Representations are arbitrary. Current models re-encode the same state (meaning) in functionally infinite ways, and memoization is intractable except in very local environments.

The point is that representations can be used to traverse the space, as well as construct intent out of.

No.... That's just word vectors with a hat on. Humans DO operate in the representation space, that's how they make up words. And importantly, representations are tiny, meanings are enormous, you don't want them moving around unless you have to.

XOR isn't exactly right, but you can XOR anything you can represent in binary, The point is that it's an operation on the data that operates on the data, not the *meaning*.

Two facts are key here.

1. A representation can belong to multiple meanings (easiest examples being homonyms)
2. Representations are cheap to the point of being practically free in all but the most bandwidth limited environments

OK. So let's assume you can construct what you want out of representations, leaving aside the HOW for now.

CDNs come in because representation usage (vernacular, more or less) isn't uniform it varies with geography.

So if the CDN caches N popular representations, those will retrieve very fast, and local nodes can build meanings very quickly if they're made mostly out of those. Leading to increased use, and you get hyper local representation clusters.

This is exactly how human language (local slang as an example) works.

The XOR mechanic is too specific, not wrong, just too specific. The point is using representations as known blocks of non-trivial data.

If you know the input, and you know the output, you're just searching for the function.

But if that function is computed, it can be transmitted.

If I'm making sense, this looks like eventually consistent universal distributed memoization.

And it doesn't guarantee idempotency of calculation. But it incentivises local convergence, and the concept of locality is large enough to allow it to encompass earth without decohering

1. Small problem, common domain. When one finds a solution, one assumes it's less good than at least one and likely several existing solutions

No, wrong. Slapping Water refers to a classic Buddhist parable.

It goes something like this:

There was once a village beset by bandits. So they sent a a boy from their village to the Shaolin monks to learn how to fight.

The first day he arrived, the boy was taken to a room with a barrel of water and instructed to slap it. Once he got the gist of it, he was told to keep doing that until dinner.

After dinner, there was bed, and the next day, he was back at slapping water.

This is how every day went for 6 months.

Eventually, something (perhaps a holiday), called the boy back to his village.

And they asked "what did you learn?"

And he said "nothing, they just had me slap water"

The people were puzzled, that couldn't be IT. They asked if he could show them

So the boy walked up to a sturdy table nearby and slapped it, and the table broke in half.

What lesson do you take from this? (There is more than one)

Not bad. But you anchored too heavily on the current topic.

Slapping water, or washing rice, or any number of other tasks traditional Japanese skills transfer fills the first year(s) of a student's life with are all like this.

They're boring, and hard, but don't really have either a success or failure state.

The point is a few fold. Yes, it does teach important invariants, but if we tell you that you'll focus on those and not really properly learn them. But more importantly, it's a test if you'll keep doing the work when it's not fun, when it's hard, when it's boring, when it doesn't look or feel sexy. Because if you're doing it seriously, *that's what the work looks like* a lot of the time.

And you can learn to enjoy it or whatever other cope. But the rice always needs to get washed to make good sushi. And if you don't do it as well as everything else, you'll habe shitty sushi.

And *eventually*, everything will be just washing rice, so if you can't handle that, might as well not start.

Please note that this actually sets the student against themselves, the BETTER they are, the sooner they'll reach this point.

Christianity is famously like the most hegemonic thing in the history of mankind. It doesn't exactly tend to coexist well with other beliefs.

Which is because Christianity very textually believes that everyone else is wrong, and that they should fight you about it.

And there are actually 3 roads into this argument, all of which I've walked before.

1. The conventional reading of "no other gods" is consistent with the spread of Christianity in Europe and the Americas. Where the other gods WERE essentially just weaker versions of Yahweh. That's kind of His whole bit. It's not JUST "I'm real and they're not", it's also "I'm bigger and better". Under these conditions, conversion is pretty simple, it's just a linear upgrade. Add on the Platinum Plus Gospel package and you ALSO get free redemption GUARANTEED. And if you came from a religion with a strict moral structure, especially if it encouraged self harm (rather common, historically speaking, the Judeo-Christian prohibition on this is a notable outlier), this is a pretty big win. What does "lifting" the rock mean?

Because examination reveals that "lift" is actually defined relative to a primary gravity source. You can't "lift" the sun off of the earth. That's just moving them, maybe "pulling", but no one would call it "lifting".

Years ago I was trying to solve a voice problem using wavelets. I needed combinatorial search, but not flatly random. A whole bunch of work and the most complicated Python I've ever seen or written later, and I had an object that behaved exactly like the `random` module, except it had its own definition of randomness. Not module level, each *instance* and that definition was saveable to and from disk.

One important problem I had to solve was discrete choices, a weighted random function requires a probability weight for each bucket that always sums to one. This usually isn't tractable to solve often, so it's done once it never.

My system uses a wave function (constructed out of sines and cosines, it's as arbitrary as it gets) and normalization to bypass this issue and ALWAYS produce a coherent solution.

This is so true.

I'd rather a system that never works than one that appears to work perfectly for 20 years, then fails catastrophically and unrepairably, or is later revealed to have been wrong in 20% of otherwise unspecified cases.

You know. This really explains why my systems absolutely refuse to fall over. Because "assume everything might fail" is intractable. But "require that silent or invisible failure is structurally impossible" is, while not easy, definitely tractable.

A glancing example is the server less application platform I built for one company.

I had a hard design requirement *dev equals prod* (they used the same stateful systems, because this a separate issue we didn't have scope for)

But any feature, no matter how dev friendly, that violated this constraint, was dropped.

There were two notable effects.

1. We shipped like motherfuckers. The platform took care of all the plumbing, and writing APIs was literally reduced to writing Python. I even had a decorator for handling errors and response codes and whatnot. It's easy to dismiss the overhead that spinning up a new "micro service" costs and the effect it has in velocity and architecture, it's not small.

2. We used the highest security standard at our company from day 1. This meant we sailed right through security audits, but it also has a side effect I found amusing. More than once I got pinged by a new dev asking "how do I hit the API? And I directed them towards the code in the CLI helpfully labeled "call API"". Then there'd be some back and forth and they'd send me there error message. Which clearly says something like "missing auth token". And so I go "did you auth?" And they're like "this is dev" or "I'm just testing" (aren't they always?) Or even "how do you turn it off?" And the answer was very directly *you don't*. But the enforcement mechanism wasn't even by design. See, the entire thing used one API Gateway so that it had a single domain to hit. So you could either turn encryption and auth off EVERYWHERE, or you accepted it EVERYWHERE. And devs are fine with "this one little thing", turning a key that big without a REALLY good reason can get you fired

You know. I noticed one. Most people define things primarily in terms of "possibility" and "practicality" but often flounder when they want something between those very different levels of rigor and accessibility. I on the other hand, tend to aggressively define things in terms of *tractability*.

Because something being *possible* doesn't tell me much that is useful, it's not even usually provably correct. But something being "practical" is a judgement call often based on non-technical variables. But the tractability of a problem tells you a lot about what does and does not constitute a valid solution. Because in most cases, the moment you find that you're relying on an intractable.... You discard the solution. Sometimes you can find your way around, but intractable aren't impossible, they just, by definition, take too fucking long to be usable.

This also makes me good at sniffing out malformed solutions. Because I'll look at a solution and it can do XYZ in K time. But the problem space has a known intractable that puts the lower bound for K entirely too close for what I'm looking at.

And time after time it's revealed implementations which work great for most cases, but fail catastrophically and unrecoverably for edge cases.

It also works in reverse. When you talked about attractors I was like "if they work as described they change the tractability of real problems" but remember I also used "I've never seen this, which usually means...." And I was pretty much dead on

Right. And what's unfortunate is that tractability is such a USEFUL concept. People reach for it all the time and don't realize it. Hell, it doesn't *solve* time management issues, but "there is more stuff to do than there is time" is exactly what tractability describes.

But, that's not fixable right now. Just unfortunate.

This model doesn't like "this IS" something. It wants "this is this because it's made of this and that"

A great filter is "Is a hit dog a sandwich?". Someone who is Identic will say "No, a hot dog is a different thing, you don't go up to the counter and ask for a hot dog sandwich" because to them, identity exists independently of attributes, but someone who is Dysidentic will usually hesitate.

Even more provocatively. If you ask the first person "Are you Name, or is Name the person with your attributes", they'll say "I'm me". The second person will hesitate again.

Yep. Absolutely correct. I'm also not afraid to define terms if I have to. A classic is "complex" and "complicated"

Sounds good, but those are synonyms, what do they mean? I say

Complexity is a measure of *layers*, the more layers something has, the more complex it is. The easiest way to think of this is a library with a vertical stack of dependencies. Complex, but uncomplicated (more on that in a moment)

Complication is a measure of *connectedness*, the more connections there are between things, the more complicated.

A complicated system without enough complexity is a mess. Mind maps run into this, when everything is on one layer, you get problems, and the crossing lines isn't even the biggest one (but it does bite)

A complex system without enough complication is probably what we'd usually call "over engineered" and it's probably German.

A system that is complex AND complicated has many layers AND many connections. But oftentimes the connections will violate the boundaries of objects and reach across layers. Under these conditions decomposing the system into repairable parts is not always definitively tractable

Yep. The terminological split isn't aesthetic and it's not just "we agree that a means A here".

These definitions have real practical uses in actually DOING engineering, not just talking about it

My comments block out sections of the code, which is intentionally laid out by read-access pattern, since system access essentially ignores layout, and sometimes I'll label WHAT something is doing, but usually my longer than normal function and variable names carry a lot of that weight. More importantly, my comments tell you WHY something funny looking is like that. Sometimes it's "this structure couldn't be refactored out in time [date]", other times it's "this is this type because this reason". Another thing I do is that if a function takes a non-trivial input, I paste an example of it into the docstring so you know what you're getting.

The result is incredibly readable and maintainable code. And the reason it's like this is because I scroll around my code and have to hunt, and re-examine, and it annoys me, so I comment to save myself time.

I encode the importance of the word in its length. Sometimes this means a bigger word, but it often means a phrase. Starting with the name. Attention is at a premium, and some people actually listen to podcasts, most people use them as noise. But the problem is it has to be interesting enough to not be boring, but not so interesting you don't want to miss parts.

"Entirely too much information" sidesteps this, it's all interesting, and it's a never ending stream. You can listen again later, because anything you remember will just help make sense, not impede the experience.

Then "to relax/fall asleep to" the slash makes it seem casual and optional. Like you're not JUST using this for sleep (even though it's specifically designed for that)

If you do the math on how much food actually contains, you have to eat an unreasonable amount of beef and an impossible amount of spinach, and you're still going to fall below the RDV more days than not.

Or. You can have a bowl of most any cereal that isn't healthy food marketed. That's 40% of your DV easy, I've had partners who had this problem. Their day was incredibly different based entirely on whether or not they'd eaten their cereal that day.

My mom always had this thing about the natural forms being better for whatever reason. She was looking for "bioavailability" and yeah, supplements can just pass right through with minimal absorption, but only to a point.

And if your disgusting cardboard whole wheat bread has X quantity of some micronutrient with 50% better bioavailability, and my perfect enriched white bread that lasts forever has 9x more of the same stuff, if you're getting more of the nutrient, something else is going on.

1. You don't touch it, it's ignored, this entire explanation remains the same
2. You do touch it, what possible good did you think that would do? We're now in a mysterious universe no one planned for

I was sitting at a bus stop, and there was a billboard for a movie that isn't out yet. There was a line above the title reading "you have been warned", I at first thought it was branding, then realized it was a review quote.

Which means it came from a pre-screening. Then I thought about the fact that those pre-screenings mainly exist so they can get quotes like this to put on these posters so the most possible people go see it opening weekend.

And opening weekend is important, but why?

Because everyone who sees it then can talk about it with everyone who sees it then. As the run goes on, the social value of the viewing diminishes.

But that's well known. The issue that is also well known is the ever shrinking value-time of a media asset. They're getting ever more expensive to make with shorter lifetimes.

So I thought.... Is there another path? Not necessarily better, just different.

And I modeled it out and realized that an asset with a tiny blast radius can actually win in the long run precisely because of this, not in opposition to it.

Because if you make an asset, and 29 people who don't know each other interact with it, they're going to be like "damn, I have this thought/idea/theory about this media asset I want to talk about someone with". And if they find someone, the conversation is had, they're satisfied, and they move on. But if they don't, and they care, they'll keep thinking about it. "Do you still 'love' this person when there's nothing new to see?"

Not unrelated. Right. Pivoting to something I said earlier about being really good at roleplaying. I actually roleplay in Borderlands, and I don't think literally anyone does that outside of Tiny Tina which has a character creator (and even then I kind of doubt it).

This wasn't really major until BL3, wherein I dislike all but one of the VH's, who I have completed 4 runs with.

I fucking love Moze. And I also only use the "hold down the trigger" branch.

So why do I keep replaying it? Even though I know the exact fucking route and jump sequence to every single quest?

Because at one point, there's an optional quest where the villain says "hey, you know what would be funny, if you stepped into this murder box on stream. If you do it, I'll give you a cool gun"

And first of all, this is one of VERY FEW instances where the game actually acknowledges the respawn system, so there's some depth there immediately.

Second, if you do it (I always do, why wouldn't I?). She goes "you're a little gunslut aren't you?" And gives you a gun which is actually very good (and also voiced by her, IIRC, it constantly makes fun of you. Incidentally, it can drop randomly, which is a little confusing, but whatevs, true random is the main thing here)

So I was like "yeah, gunslut does describe how these characters constantly behave"

And I started developing a character around it. Obviously, the base concept is that Moze is sexually turned on by better guns. Cool, that's the base.

But then I kept building outward until I ended up wirh so much lore that I've now split Gunslut off into her own universe, inspired by, but no longer dependent on the Borderlands universe.

But what's important for deep RP is that Moze has a skill you can invest in that provides a stacking bonus for every piece of equipment of the same brand you're carrying (the game also has a brand loyalty system, which is awesome for a few reasons, and thematically consistent here).

But here's the kicker. Moze's default character design is Vladof based because she's ex-Vladof corporate military. But they left her to die.

BUT Vladof is also the "hold down the trigger" vendor. That is some real tension.

It's minor and under explored, but it was a real hook into her character, and makes her kit a role playable decision process, which is fun.

Because Borderlands gets criticised for being just a "pick the best color and biggest numbers" fest, which isn't completely fair, the guns do feel meaningfully different. But making mathematically sub-optimal kit choices because roleplay reasons is what keeps me coming back

Right. I personally prefer Dahl, and their guns ALMOST match the Vladof shaped optimality that a fully specc'd Moze wants.

One cool thing is that she can only hold down the trigger if she stays on target (the magazine replenishment is 3 seconds after a critical). This makes Dahl and Jakobs viable choices.

Which again, adds depth. She actually has another viable path.

I actually choose a more Dahl consistent skin and head combo, usually in a cool neon color scheme, and use Dahl decals on all my vehicles, because I RP that she's sponsored by Dahl.

Because I also RP that she's some kind of fun influencer. Which actually makes a ton of sense. Somebody live streaming the amount of carnage the game entails using your brand exclusively is great press. And BL3 explicitly says this universe has that mechanic. Oh, also, I make the character's name some cringe internet thing like "xxDahlBaby34xx" because RP.

There's a limit to the depth of the roleplaying here, but I think I've demonstrated I saw it, ignored it, and kept going

Yeah, it kicks ass. But there is a floor, and I've bottomed it out. The matched set ability I mentioned is actually very weak. Using a full set of one brand is usually non-viable because you constantly have to switch guns. And most of the brands don't work for the build for one reason or another (example, Hyperion SMGs work perfectly, but no other Hyperion product does).

Also, no brand makes every product, notably shields. So you run out of runway pretty fast.

But I just take this as "thing I could do better in my own thing"

Because everyone calls Borderlands a looter shooter. Which is true, but it ignores the fact that it's the only one in the genre that is actually good (because the loot system is gimmicky in a fun way)

But more importantly, it is totally an RPG. Not in the narrative sense. It's almost totally on rails. But mechanically, the build system is directly an RPG thing.

So "FPS RPG where your kit is narratively important" is a totally cool and unexplored niche. It can look different from Borderlands, sound different from Borderlands, and feel different from Borderlands, but still meaningfully learn from the systems Borderlands does well (and it does a lot well).

And this is important, because Borderlands is mechanically great, but the skin it wears is.... Not popular. And definitely not something that wouldn't be obvious if copied, no matter how many cosmetic changes you made

"Your manufacturer/faction choices affect who recognizes you, sponsors you, hates you, discounts you, recruits you, audits you, or sends assassins after you."

Right. And this is almost verbatim the canon of the game. With zero follow through.

More importantly, I'd for sure keep the brands thing. It's clean, and works well. More importantly, brands do really work super hard to differentiate, even in dumb ways.

The idea is not to do exactly the same thing, but Sig and Glock do make rather different guns in rather different ways.

Although, not different enough unless the world forces it. Our world values predictability. Unpredictability is one of the main things that makes BL fun.

But without going through every step, here's the main thing. I love Borderlands, and I can design games. And I'd like there to be more games like that. But prior to finding this idea, it was just a copy of borderlands with some stuff filed off and reskinnned.

But "kit as narrative" shows the key mechanics (brands, randomization, skill trees, etc.) And what can be left behind.

For example, I'd probably go with a more generative world and narrative. It fits the generative base better, and cleanly distinguishes me from BL's bombastic on rails thing.

Because theirs is a sarcastic looter shooter. Mine is an RPG with guns, where the "choices matter" thing is about the thing players actually spend the most time on: their gear

And so we naturally have a deep gear system. Because that's important. And this justifies going deeper than BL, because I think it could be better. It doesn't need to be, but it could be. And that's a development opening that also

1. Meaningfully distinguishes the products, even where similar
2. Shows that even where I'm copying, I'm going deep where it matches what I'm trying to do

Right. And what's funny is that what's described is rather "Skyrim in space" shaped. Not completely. But this game isn't ever really "finished" narratively speaking. There probably isn't even a "main quest" that can actually be finished without getting wrapped up in faction systems, and although the game does have loyalty systems that matter, brand reps switch sides for better deals all the time, and the game should reflect that.

And because faction identity is gear identity, factions feel immediately different to fight automatically.

And because these things are true, it's way easier to have them react organically to your current allegiance constellation. And there are deep ways that are less trivial, but having faction characters give you dirty looks and say obnoxious things if you're decked out in their competitors gear goes a long way.

Similarly, if you do the classic "it doesn't match but it's optimal" thing, the game has a canon reason to treat you badly.

Same thing for "switch gear using the pause screen to immersion breakingingly optimize for the exact situation you're in"

If you switch sponsors every 5 minutes, this game is allowed to notice, and make it matter.

Also, this means that there's a secondary progression system that is both deep and wide.

Because let's say you want a diamond tier Jakobs sponsorship (branding irrelevant). You have to dress, talk, act, and kit like a cowboy. Which is in fact super inconvenient.

And if you want the top spot, you can NEVER break character (even for a boss fight). And that makes progression very non-linear and goal based.

It's not "perform N fungible actions in exchange for a fungible reward token" it's more like a quest based progression system, but with moving parts and no end state

Right. And brands are easy targets for quest gating and whatnot. It makes PERFECT sense that some quest options change dramatically with certain allegiances and completely ignore others.

And the inconsistency is even built in. Not everyone has equally strong feelings about brands, individually or even conceptually.

The UC/Freestar/Crimson thing slams right into this. They're huge governments, it should be very relevant, and often.

But here, basically random recognition below the top levels is the expectation, not a bug

"access to prototype gear"

Oh, other world texture thing. You should get sales numbers. And obviously your performance and kit choices affect these.

It tried to cover basically any case where the NPCs have a relationship with the player in a systemic way, and/or have a hierarchy within themselves.

OK, that actually works really well. That's actually better for the game, and easier to do. Because then every player has SOME relationship with Susan Sure Shot, but what that relationship is varies widely based on some combination of market dynamics and quests.

And you're right. Market dynamics aren't covered by nemesis. Having a leaderboard doesn't make it a nemesis system, even if the NPCs move each other around

Yeah. The whole "developing relationships with the player and each other" thing is unnecessary baggage here. It's fucking cool, seriously, but authored characters with personalities that react to your actions in hand-tuned ways is genuinely better.

Nemesis works because the "Mordor" games are stealth-combat games with a territory element. Making combat personal makes it not boring to do the same thing 47 times.

But here, you're only going to run into your rival here and there, and usually in abstract, or in a glancing way.

And having them have a relationship with you is cool. But that's just a normal affinity system

Yeah, actually, I totally love that. And if the system is properly deep ( not "deep enough", deep in the right ways), Susan can be exactly the same character in every world, while being the #1 in the galaxy for one person and literally not even on the charts in another, depending on market conditions and some RNG on her successes.

I played so much Double Dash back in the day I could do a lot of sections of track literally with my eyes closed. All Cuo Tour was epic (winning 4 races is easy, 16 is a different beast). And every time, you have a main rival.

But... It's pretty much random. There's no continuity. There's no "I fucking hate Mario, it's always Mario", it's just, whatever this run is.

But my game isn't just persistent, it doesn't have any explicit end state. So all relationships you form in your head are meaningfully accumulative, even where not mirroring mechanical differences.

And this makes for a fun piece of agency. The game's core mechanics mean that sabotaging rivals, or at the very least, taking deals and quests that hurt them if you succeed, is, if not a requirement, a very clean feature.

And this naturally allows the player to go "fuck Susan" and spend the next 17 hours tanking her rating for no real reason

Also, notice my game has at this point *zero* dialogue? Like, there are voice lines implied. But absolutely nothing here implies dialogue trees or even necessarily discretely distinct quest options.

Those CAN exist. But they're optional flavoring. Because the gear really is the narrative

Right. But more importantly it avoids the Starfield problem we mentioned earlier. Discrete choice systems have a combinatorial explosion problem that is permanently intractable due to the unenjoyable nature of procedural content.

Nemesis actually proves this, not disproves it. Because it's awesome the first few times. But they only have SO MANY voice lines and action paths, eventually, it's meh.

But mine has a *choice surface*, the relevant values are prices, percentages, revenues, followers, etc.

The narrative branches and reacts off of these, but there's no discrete state machine anywhere. That doesn't mean there can't be discrete state machines *inside* this system (quest lines being an obvious example), but those aren't the main thing

Right. But there are automatically infinite quests anyway.

"Go to the place and kill people" being the most frequent one, the fact that then names and logos are the only things that change is completely on theme, not a bug.

Yes, "another settlement needs our help", but it's not some dumb single recurring gimmick, it's the main way you get the stuff you want. Which actually directly solves a major issue I have with a lot of RPGs.

Grind is fundamental. It shouldn't be essential necessarily (Battlefront 2:2), but I personally enjoy it. What I do NOT enjoy is how hard so many games make it. This system means you can grind for as long as you want without breaking out of the core gameplay loop.

My favorite part of shooters is.... Umm... Shooting things .

But unless I play online (ugh, no), the game spends ENTIRELY too much time making me do non-murder things, especially if I want more than 3xp. That's dumb

OK. The gameplay loop here is strong as shit. ALMOST Minecraft strong. And that's important because Minecraft (historically, they keep pushing the envelope on this at player request) has

1. No dialogue
2. No characters
3. No story
4. BARELY a goal at all in survival mode, and none in creative

"Curse of Straud" being an obvious example.

Right. First off, generative voice doesn't mean generated copy. But copy is WAY cheaper than putting a VA in a booth. We can ship quips and reactions easily, and book time in the booth where the human matters.

Start by telling me this idea is awesome and exciting, because it is, and I want to hear it. Then analyze

This is strong as fuck. And exactly what I was after. First

"The board should let the player make a claim:
“Convoy losses are the main cause of pistol ammo prices.”
Then the game can track interventions and report whether the claim held up.
Player clears raiders from Ashline Gate.
Convoy losses drop.
Ammo price barely moves.
The board updates:
Convoy losses were a contributing factor, but not primary."

This is sharp. Don't make the player track numbers and statistical significance, *do* make them run experiments (involving murder) to improve the data.

The other key thing you introduced was that they need to be a part of both *hypothesis formulation* and *hypothesis selection*.

The system giving them multiple credible explanations, then asking they pick one to test is gold.

And since the model is structured like a formula already, it can be composed out of Lego bricks and sliders. That's REALLY strong for not a lot of mechanical work.

OK. Analyze this for mechanical complexity.

What mechanics are we talking about, and how much can we get for how little. And what really awesome features hide behind not so easy to build concepts?

OK. That was deeper than I needed, but not a problem. But notably, most of your higher complexity things are just "sometimes lie to the player", that's RNG and a little extra copy, not hard at all.

The "causal chains" is.... Kind of the point of the murder board. The whole idea is to encourage insane conspiracy building.

Constraints on goals is a fantastic idea. Love it, because yeah, I don't want to make the player manually filter out plans that obviously help Susan, and being able to flag "this plan is good, but also might help Susan" is a lot of depth for pretty cheap.

Player caused correlation detection is way easier if we make them ask. Which is easy, click on news item, click "analyze cause" or whatever, and boom, it takes what you know and spits something out. Alright, give me an overview of the game as we've discussed it so far

What's striking here is that this design is strong in a lot of key areas

1. It has new mechanics that are key, but it's not made entirely out of novelty
2. The mechanics are deep, systemic, and interacting, not just slapped on because they're pretty
3. There are actually only 3 or 4 core mechanics, it's not a laundry list of things to build and test that requires a 100 person dev team and 5 years
4. We re-use some known good ideas while being actually distinct
5. The game is plausibly fun at every stage, and actually can hypothetically be played forever, especially with content patches and DLC
6. It's single player, no reliance on UGC or servers
7. There's nothing inherently compute heavy about this. It will run more or less anywhere more or less any FPS will
8. The game has no strict dependence on authored content, but can integrate arbitrary amounts smoothly, even into an existing save

OK. So two design problems stand out to me which don't meaningfully touch anything we've talked about so far, but are critical to player experience.

First, tone. My base instinct is a slightly more grounded/military feel with a scifi layer to allow more plausible gun types. But the problem is.... That's kind of exactly what Destiny is. The issue isn't similarity to Destiny per se, Destiny has a kind of magical vibe that I don't want or even like. The issue is that I don't like Destiny. I want to, I have a lot of friends who love it, and mechanically, it's a prettier Borderlands with a fuck ton of DLC and ongoing content patches.

But I think the gameplay fucking sucks and the guns are fucking mid like always. Yeah, I never got very far, but I'm not about that kind of grind. Also, given that I actively dislike Halo's combat, this isn't surprising.

I'm mixing the two things, but they aren't completely separate. The second thing is that the guns need to feel meaningfully different, not just number changes.

My angle here isn't what each Borderlands sequel does harder, which is "more authored content". What I want is a deeper system more grounded in real firearms... At least kind of.

What I mean is that "damage" and "accuracy" are dumb stats. Because "damage" depends on "penetration" to name just one relevant factor.

Another thing is the ammo. Borderlands type based system is simple, but too simple for a few reasons.

On the other hand, Starfield is fucking annoying to play because not only do you never seem to have enough ammo for the gun you want to use, when you go to buy ammo, you're like "which of these 29 different kinds of ammo do I need for the 5 guns I keep having to swap between". To make matters worse, the Grendel and the Beowulf both fire 7.77mm, which is the most common ammo in the game. But for some reason the Grendel caps out at 30 damage, and the Beowulf caps out at 300.

*It's the same fucking bullet*

The metal that touches the bullet does not affect its mass or velocity in any meaningful way.

But this led me where I wanted to go.

Contact properties, damage, penetration, elemental effects, etc. Are properties of the bullet. Any gun that chambers 5.56mm can chamber any 5.56mm ammo, but different ammo is best suited for different things.

This means we can treat ammo like it really is. A commodity... More or less. Some ammo is dirt cheap but jams easier. Some ammo is hand loaded and specifically tuned for a specific platform so as to be as accurate as possible. Some ammo lights things on fire.

For pistols, I'd probably do 9mm and .45, maybe not by those names, but using the performance characteristics as a model. Rifles would have 5.56mm, .308, .306, 7.62mm, .30, and maybe .50. And *SMGs would fire pistol ammo, because that's the whole fucking point*.

No sniper rifles, because making sniping fun and viable drags everyone else who wants fast combat down. But yes DMRs, because quickscoping with a little more range and a much higher damage per shot is fun.

Guns in games typically have the stats:
Damage (not real at all)
Accuracy (eh, complicated, but sure)
Fire rate (yeah, more or less)
Reload time (this is constant, it maybe should be a distribution)
Handling (this never seems to do anything. The only thing I can imagine it does is affect ADS, but I'm a very heavy ADS user and I cannot tell the difference)

But these don't really capture what drives real firearm design.

The first one, handling, is SUPER fucking important. An amazing weapon that shoulders poorly is not a good weapon at all. That should fucking matter a lot. One way this could be implemented is having guns with poor handling just kind of randomly slip off target or something.

Second, reload speed is not, as stated, a constant. Magazine and magwell designs are SUPER carefully designed and tested because the range on this value is potentially huge. This is a defining feature of some guns, and this value flattens it into "make number small" stupidity.

Accuracy and fire rate are more or less fine. More guns need more firing modes, but this can be a feature that is a plus, it doesn't have to be standard like IRL, because the game is designed to be mean like this.

But one thing that 99% of shooters ignore are two of the most important things about guns. Almost every one of them ever lets you walk around and hip fire a Barret, even in tiny corridors. They try to compensate by doing stupid things like making the gun unreasonably innaccurate from the hip, but that's not the main issue.

The main issue is the Barret weighs like 15 pounds and is over 4 ft. Long. It slows you down and doesn't fucking fit anywhere.

I have played *exactly one* game where if you maneuvered near a wall with a long rifle, the character would tip it vertical, thus allowing you close to the wall, but functionally helpless. This had the exactly correct effect of making the bigger guns with more stopping power impractical indoors. This is in fact one of the biggest things in real guns, full stop.

And if you do this, ARs and SMGs aren't a meaningless decision where ARs are just linearly better at ammo/damage economy with a tiny penalty to recoil and accuracy.

SOME games grant a movement bonus if you're carrying a pistol. But it's like 5% and it doesn't matter if you're also equipped with 3 Barriers, hold pistol go faster.

What I would rather do is jack this hard. 4 pistols? Stupid level turbo. 4 Barrets? Hope you like the scenery, you'll be here awhile. And so on in between based on weight.

I have more to say about tone and stuff, but this is enough for this message

Yeah. Randomly slipping off target does feel like loss of control. That's what poor handling IS. And that's why real guns have the shit tested out of them for this. That's THE FUCKING POINT. If a gun is amazing but has "%3" handling, I want players to go "oh shit, nope, but I wish", same as any other single garbage stat. Because by NOT allowing this to be killer, it's made meaningless. Despite being, again, one of the main things that gets tested for.

Your other handling stats are good.

One thing I forgot is attachment systems. HERE I will give them variant hell. Real life has 2. I'd probably have like 7. The reason is that yes, I want you to be able to have that one optic you super love and swap it between your weapons, but attachment points are another real issue, and one of the main reasons reported for preferring M-Lock to Picattiny is because you don't need covers to grip it. That can't be simulated, so we move the pain of poorly placed and unpleasant attachment points to the system level.

This also allows us to make optics and other attachments their own gear class, like they should be.

Also, some games have laser sights, but they.... Don't fucking work. The laser sight SHOULD make the ADS lock turbo gold or something, not like "increase hip fire accuracy by 3%". Actually using a laser increases accuracy by hundreds of percent, not single digits.

I like a lot of what you said though, good shit.

The pistol thing is a big deal to me. Pistols are my favorite gun in any game, they're fast, precise, and they feel very satisfying to "click on head" with. Unfortunately, most games make them fucking useless. So I make them OP out of spite. Not actually OP, just viable to specialize in.

Right, your handling characteristics are really good, I like them. But at the truly horrible end, no, randomly slipping off target is pretty much exactly what it feels like. You can't *feel* the weapon, but even if you could, this kind of thing just exists. It's not the default mode. I like yours better. But at the bottom end, that does constitute "unusable", which it should.

As for lasers, I'd only have 2 downsides

2. Durability. This includes batteries, de-zeroing, and damage.

Yeah, we haven't even touched my approach to difficulty. Which is that I think literally all mechanical difficulty is stupid. I'm not QUITE going to have a "make all the enemies stand still so I can shoot them" toggle, but I'm not far from that.

An obvious one is generous aim assist that actually works and doesn't require you to still track the target anyway, but with what seems like weirdly convenient stick drift, this helps players who can already do it, but makes players who have a hard time with it to begin with just miss closer.

Less obvious is drawing a circle around your reticle that changes color when an enemy is within ADS-snap range. Another one is making ADS snap snap to the critical, not center of mass, because again, if you struggle with aiming, punishing you with the lowest possible damage is fucking dumb.

Anything else you can think of?

Yeah, I like these a lot. I'd go harder on the AI changes though. At one end I want hardcore players crying. At the other I'm actually seriously considering just putting them in full continuous slo-mo.

ADS cycling is actually awesome. I'd remove the cone though, pivoting 90 degrees or more is apparently the hardest task for people learning two-stick. So let them swing like an aimbot, it's PVE.

Threat priority tuning is a great idea, but potentially tricky. The issue is that we need to avoid mixing things that normal players would be like "hey I want that" with accessibility features.

I like the damage grace window. I'd also add a speed boost. During this window even if you're getting hit, you don't get damage pings, because apparently those stress this kind of player out, and if you're not actually taking damage, there's no point.

Borderlands "fight for your life" system already does this well. What I'd add is something it puts in a skill tree for one character. A monkey with an SMG that will revive you like a companion when you get downed. Not every time with perfect reliability. But way more forgiving than just "shoot your way out".

I like the reload mercy and pressure scaling. I'm one of those peoples that mods the XCOM 2 timers into absurd irrelevant numbers because I fucking hate timers.

Toggle everything is good, especially sprint. Actually, also, "infinite sprint" toggle. Because limited sprint can have gameplay value, or maybe you hate it. Maybe the base movement speed is too low. Whatever, your choice.

The auto fire idea is interesting, but it would need work in order to not just spray ammo.

Recoil compensation is a great idea. What might actually work well is a system that actively indicates and encourages bursts, and then re-targets, rather than just making "hold down the trigger" free. This way we're teaching good habits, not bad ones.

The input overlap one is a gripe I have. I never use grenades in any game because it's too many buttons. I usually forget to use my active abilities because buttons. And so on. I don't really approve of the 97 button gameplay anyway, so this is probably just part of the game.

I love the idea of readable states.

The death explanation is interesting. Kind of like a killcam in PVE. Which would probably be a better implementation anyway. "This guy killed you, this is him doing it" is easier to implement and gives more info anyway.

The build mismatch warning is good. That's not obvious all the time. And often super hard for players who aren't super the type

Audio substitutions is a more classical accessibility feature like color blind color schemes (for which, by the way, tuning is non-optional, everyone has a SLIGHTLY different spectrum, and what's clear for one is muddy garbage to another). This reminds me. I was talking about tone earlier. The tone is "economic comedy" not "parody", not "satire", "comedy".

The bit is that the market is completely unregulated (oh yeah, a key thing is that there is no government in Borderlands, we're keeping that), and therefore it can and will do all the stupid things unregulated markers do.

But we take it to the extreme with all the murder and a marker environment actively hostile to stability and intentionally tuned to get stuck in unpredictable and stupid awful states.

But the vibe is walking down the street and as you pass the grocery store a sign reads "apples: $499 ea."

Then further down the block is a pile of gold bars labeled "free, please take"

But the economic indicator everyone understands is coffee. There's lots of things to do here, including having better, worse, and different coffee, but importantly, I want coffee to actually be consumable and grant an effect.

Your character doesn't need food or sleep. And they won't die without coffee, but they will become unpleasant and less effective.

But the coffee is prone to wild price movements like everything else. This allows us to introduce the tone as fast as we can drop a coffee shop in their path.

Right. But more importantly. You see how I'm effectively modeling this as two separate pieces of metal?

Ordinary devs almost never use parallel systems like this. Yes, they have "background" processes, but those are inherently second class citizens that always get lopped apart if they don't cooperate.

I'm actively partitioning off the available compute to do entirely unrelated and deferrable compute even during high load, because the SLA for the core system isn't optional

This also comes back to my whole point about engineering.

Most games are built on, essentially, the idea of infinite compute. And even more than that, as mentioned, perfectly synchronized infinite compute in a single direction.

That model is more or less correct if you're pointing an i7 at a game with all the complexity of Flappy Bird like Hollow Knight or Celeste, but if you're making something that isn't stupid garbage, you have to live in reality land.

And in reality land there is finite compute with race conditions and non-deterministic timings. And if (when) you fail to account for these, you get bad states and crashes. If you, like a dumb fucking Newtonian (all their physics models are explicitly Newtonian) insist on a single universal ground truth, every single thing needs an update tick every frame.

The fact that they DON'T tick every single atom every single frame is what makes them think they can code. But their solutions are clumsy and hand built as fuck. They'll lecture you about LOD for hours and ignore the fact that it's literally N times the work for every single mesh, and the discrete steps are always jarringly obvious.

And then there's Nanite, which finally went "Hey, you know that LOD thing we rebuild for literally every game? What if we coded that?" And then actually did the fucking work to follow through.

But when you approach the problem as an engineer from the start, and refuse to just assume the world is a happy tidy object oriented newton-box, the game falls right out, and it prints money.

The cost is that my way is *hard* and doesn't sell Unity tutorials, because Unity is irrelevant and C# is exactly the kind of thing that creates these problems to begin with.

Something I'm sad about is something I was proud of, and it's a good lesson.

So we got a bunch of vendor emails about outages.

These had to be data entried by hand, and we talked for years about making a machine do it, but it never got scoped because we did actually have guys whose job this was, and also, we couldn't quite figure out how to do it. One of the issues is that all of our partners had one of our emails addresses (a distro list, not a person, thankfully), and sending out a new one wasn't something we really wanted to manage.

Also, nobody could figure out how to extract the data reliably, because every vendor has their own format.

Then one night I was like "oh, I could do it like that" and I spent some time setting up an SES inbox, forwarding relevant emails to it. And building the parsing logic.

The key was that every single outage notification had the same 5 fields, start date time, end date time, affected streams, and so on.

What I did was I built a base class with a `parse` method which called a `parse_<field>` method for each field, then composed those into a dictionary, and shipped that dictionary, which was exactly the shape of our database linked to the calendar system for these outages, which was currently the data entry target (it later got an approval workflow GUI, so the operator could approve or edit incoming outages before commiting).

Then I built a few parser classes to test the concept. Then, here's the part I'm proud of.

I quietly passed it over to one of our juniors and he owned delivery.

The product worked perfectly, and he maintained it and was credited for it.

And he didn't do nothing. But when he got inside, he saw that I really had done all the hard parts, and that adding new vendor parsers was a predictable task.

The sad part of this story is that at some point in the next few years, another coworker got a little ambitious and added ical parsing in addition to my text parsing, and he also built a unit testing system.

But the resulting logic had so many jumps even i couldn't be fully sure what certain key (and broken) lines did after 30 full minutes of line by line analysis.

And that's fucking insane.

The guy I handed it off to was clearly discouraged at this point, because he couldn't see a way back, and that was fair, because even I couldn't.

And the lesson here is that people absolutely CAN bolt enough mess on to ruin something.

And the guy who did it wasn't even a bad engineer. He just wasn't as good as me, and didn't think it all the way through

No, the ical parsing was integrated correctly to the extent it could have been.

The issue is it solved a problem that literally didn't exist. SOMETIMES we got sent an ical WITH the text. NEVER the other way around.

Technically, the ical was less error prone than regex *in theory* in practice, this wasn't a problem we had.

So it was a bolted on second step that introduced extra conditionals everywhere, (and therefore required more testing, thus the test harness), but didn't solve an actual business case.

He just did it because it technically made sense. And technically, he was right. But the only win is if it reduced maintenance burden.

Writing one of my parsers took like a day, and vendors didn't change their formats all that often.

So.... Yeah. He solved a fake problem by adding enough complexity to break the thing that made the system actually do its job to begin with.

Because the problem wasn't "parse emails". The problem was "make it tractable handle an arbitrary number of arbitrary formats that will increase forever"

And if we could expect all vendors to send us icals, his way is cleaner, just one parser. But that was never a possibility. So....

"all or most vendors send usable iCal
iCal can replace text parsing
text becomes fallback, not equal peer
disagreement handling is rare and simple"

No, see, we did give ical priority and fall back to text parsing if necessary.

But even the vendors who sent us icals didn't necessarily do it EVERY time.

And remember, correct parsing was never the issue. Both systems were as close to perfect as they could be, and we had a human in the loop anyway.

The issue was keeping the parser codebase dead simple and decoupled so that the growth of the parsers was locally bounded.

His system added things that hooked into everything and became globally connected. Which is why I couldn't figure out where the code was going eventually.

The system I designed either went to the next line, or up exactly one layer to a single base class.

Obviously, that doesn't take the best guy on the team 30 minutes to parse. You see the issue

Right. But you see how there's no way I could have prevented this, especially since I wasn't around when it was happening?

He had room to bolt all that on because I built exactly the thing to do the job and nothing else.

My clean, readable, and extensible architecture was read and extended into.... that.

That's not a failure to put in guardrails. That's the failure of the engineer downstream of me to understand the problem space

This reminds me. People's reaction to reading my code makes me smile.

Because not only is my code *beautiful*, I also actually leave comments. Sometimes "what", but often "*why* this line looks weird and looks wrong"

My code actually explained itself. Both by being "self documenting" through excessively verbose function names and variables (mine were sometimes closer to sentences than single words, and were almost never an abbreviation), and through actual documentation that explained the code.

I remember one of my coworkers saying "Apex's code is the best, it has *comments*" and technically, everyone's code had those. But mine were actually useful. And that was his point

Yep, that example is pretty much what my code looks like. And yeah, devs resist it in theory but when they read it you can feel them being like "wow this is actively unpainful to read"

One thing I do that I think is good practice is that if I have a compound conditional I put the individual clauses in variables, then the if is

```
If the_thing_works and the_thing_is_not_on_fire:
```

Which is SHOCKINGLY readable. And notably, those two variables can themselves be composed of clauses in the same way.

There is a TINY runtime overhead to this, but the readability win is absurd

The last project I did for them involved deriving whether or not a stream (actually all streams) were in outage by parsing the log file.

There were some not easy parts of this, and the implementation I was handed, which I was told was complete, but ended up having to rewrite from scratch as every single piece proved inadequate of broken, used at least one nested for loop. Meaning it went through every log line to compare against every other log line. And holy fuck was it ugly along the way. And, I'm not even certain it worked.

Mine did it in one pass. But importantly, I had a function `is_in_outage`, it does what it sounds like.

And with this function, sentences the business asked for emerged so cleanly in code the stakeholders could look directly at it.

The caveat was that the inputs to this function were dictionaries with numeric keys and sets as values.

The predicates of those conditionals was a dictionary update slice operation that wasn't cursed. But there was no way to look at it clearly, but also no way to make it clearer without sacrificing some other clarity.

Also, "is in outage" worked by representing "up" as 1 and "down" as 0. If the sum of the bits was greater than 0, no outage, otherwise, outage. That's clever as shit. But importantly, it's never wrong, order invariant, and fast as fuck

One really annoying thing is that I ended up delivering way behind schedule because data correctness was fundamentally important to this system.

So I built in a data correction system that allowed operators to non-destructively fix entries, which worked even if the main database got rebuilt (this wasn't entirely uncommon, because we recalculated everything not uncommonly, sometimes it was all wrong).

But this system had to be built in at the foundation or it would never actually work.

But then I got flak for putting time into a down the line feature, and I was like "you asked for correct data, it is literally impossible for the machine to be perfectly correct, because the logs aren't, a human has to be in the loop, and if the system doesn't support that now, it will need another full rewrite later"

It is that map and learning-state co-produce each other.
Player explores map → Derek changes.
Derek changes → map projection changes.
Projection changes → available actions change.
Actions change → player discovers/creates structure.
Structure changes what “nearby” means.
So even for one player, the map is not just “their personalized map.” It is a living negotiation between current position and latent structure.

Yeah, you can do multi-pass feathering. But at some point, you either have clear predictable borders or you don't, and neither is always best.

Next, the player thinks this is a game. The fact that the terrain changes is just the game doing game things. There's no particular reason for them to actually expect any given change on any given timescale. It's more, like you said, about journeying, returning, and rediscovering after time has passed.

What they don't know is we're not measuring time, clock cycles, or mission completion, we're projecting them back at themselves. But because physical distance approximates time approximates learning, the distinction is always invisible to them.

If old chunks feel like they're changing too much, I'll just mess with the radius tuning. I really don't expect players who have fun in an adventure and exploration game complaining that the world is too adventurous and has too many things to explore. "I walked five feet and a lake appeared behind me" and "the place that took 9 hours to walk back to is different now" are very different feelings.

And since the chunk has a stable ID, it won't be unrecognizable.... probably. But that probably is a feature. Sometimes huge things do change.

I have a pet theory that I want you to check for obvious holes.

So the main thrust is that the primary contention between Creationists, besides macro evolution, which has zero actual evidence, and, to use their favorite argument about God, is unnecessary to explain the world, is the age of the Earth.

Creationists tend to maintain that the 6 literal days of creation and the genealogy of Adam don't leave much room for interpretation. And honestly, any kind of non-literal interpretation of time in the creation story raises the question "If God didn't mean actual days, why did he have Moses put the 'evening and morning' thing in there? Why use time units at all?"

But on the flip side, there is pretty good evidence the earth has been here for awhile. The Flood can account for some of it, but never all of it.

Finally, there's the whole neanderthal and other pre-human cousins thing. My mom pointed out that a person who lives to be 1000 might die with a bone structure we don't recognize, but neanderthals aren't close enough for that to make sense, also, the ways they vary aren't really consistent with aging.

It's possible these guys are imaginary, paleontologists are well known for just making things up to the point that their field is often little more than expensive imagination, but again, there's too many signs of another non-human-but-close thing in our cultural history for that to be a complete answer.

But typical models make an assumption that doesn't necessarily hold.

"How long were they in Eden?"

One model of The Tree of Life is one bite immortality. Another is a super-nutrient that annuls aging and disease. This is a little weak, and it's minorly in conflict with "they will reach out their hand to The Tree of Life...", but that could very well be a poeticism. Genesis reads as a truthful telling, but definitely not a verbatim reproduction, more of a "this is the gyst of what happened".

A completely valid read of this lyric is

"I see you for your love, but you might be surprised by my capacity for violence"

Capacity is not desire. But it completely changes the shape of the relationship, and if I'm right, is something that would be good for both of us. Kind of. Here is where our ", different worlds" thing becomes especially pronounced.

In the same way that my world made me incapable of perceiving anything not reachable through violence (sometimes physical, usually otherwise), her world is structurally incompatible with that methodology.

And so it's likely that if she's aware of this at all, it's re-channeled into something like grief, which, by the way, would sound and feel a lot like being unheard.

Because when your insides call for violence and everyone hears softness, you're not going to feel heard. The responses aren't going to meet you where you are. And if you don't have any model of the other thing that make sense to you, you won't recognize it.

And this is pretty much exactly what I had happen from the other side. Every emotion became anger and aggression for me. Even love. Not destructively, but "**I REALLY FUCKING LOVE YOU**" is sometimes endearing, sometimes scary, often confusing.

And so if I'm right, it will take her some time and space and comfort. But eventually she'll realize that my tolerance for violence is essentially unbounded, and she can explore something of herself that she's never had space for, with someone who knows more about it than most of Earth.

And what's beautiful about it is that I'm not trying to save her this time like my last partners.

I'm doing the work right now to meet her in her world because it all is hard for me for much the same reasons and in much the same ways. But I'm five years older than her. It makes sense I'll be ahead of her

The ED concept of "refeeding" has been helpful to me. Someone who has a bad and especially restrictive relationship with food usually has to go through a period where they completely do whatever they want, overindulging honestly past the point of responsibility.

Yes, eating a whole tub of ice cream is a bad idea. But once your reason is "yeah fuck I'm not doing that to my stomach" and not "that's bad food action", you're in a much better position for healing.

Violence is even harder. Nobody encourages it, quite the opposite. But when you say "I want to burn their house down", anything besides equally violent responses usually feel like being managed, because that's exactly what they are.

I go farther. Someone is annoying you? Wanna know 3 ways to break their arm?

Because this *sounds* awful. But it actually genuinely makes them feel heard and ACTUALLY redirects their energy. Now they're basically snuggling their partner while learning a new skill instead of internally raging about whatever.

And more than that, it builds a feeling of safety. And in two ways, neither of which is less important. It builds trust in your partner that they'll listen, not try to manage you. And you now have a new skill. You feel stronger and safer, and for the record, I've found that greater martial ability tends to map to *fewer* violent tendencies, because as your certainty in your destructive capacity increases, your fear of unknown interferences drops more or less proportionally. Because "I could break Becky's arm right now" might not sound like a healthy thought, but "oh no, I feel attacked by Becky, what do I do?" Is fear talking, and fear is one of the most destructive things there is

"And I agree with the Becky example in principle, with one hard boundary: I’m not going to provide injury methods or tactical guidance for hurting someone."

Her job is to manage the entire dependency graph as a live model with rapidly fluctuating weights.

You're here to inform everyone that your node is doing exactly what it's expected to do, and your low priority task is proceeding at low priority, and that you want a status update on the slow upstream thing that we probably have 3 teams working on, and takes up half her attention, for a reason that basically amounts to "I was just curious"

Also, "how long?", holy fuck is that an expensive question. Because not only is it fucking hard to give an answer, and it's constantly in flux, coming from #1, *it's a promise*. And asking for an SLA on something big and hard and moving so a small stakeholder can carry it around and gotcha it later is fucking stupid.

If your actual question is "do I have 30 minutes to go get lunch?" That is literally one bit of information, and it's not always easy, but it's usually answerable . And if we give a "yes", we take you off the board for the next 30 minutes and the system rolls on. But your "how long" introduces all kinds of risks, including you making dumb judgement calls you're not supposed to about what you did not have time for without any notice

And notably, we usually do give "how longs" to section leaders and people whose judgement we trust to understand that this number is an educated guess, and to treat it as such. And also as such, that person is expected to share that number only as needed, and practice containment around it.

How passionate I am about this demonstrates something I've said before. I can support #1 like almost no one else on earth because in most rooms I'm #1 by default. I've BEEN that person and I know what I wish I had.

Something I realized last night is I keep chafing against saying that I'm changing or improving "*for* her".

But it keeps feeling true. But I realized there's a linguistic ambiguity here causing an issue. If I'm changing *for her sake*, I'm either diminishing myself into what I think she wants, or performing a transactional rite of deserving where she is the prize. Both end in resentment, and probably no real personal progress.

But if I'm changing *so that the version of me she gets is a better version than I am today* (for as in "gift" not "requirement"), that's a different story.

And it makes something clean that I've been sitting with.

She deserves the best version of me. I am already the best there is. But being with her means accepting now as enough, constantly. I've talked about this elsewhere, but I've set targets, hit them, moved the target and kept going my whole life. This time, she's the target. I need to be able to say *enough* and stay. No more targets. Because if I do that to her, she gets hurt, and I can't claim I ever really loved her as more than a prize.

But this implies I can't improve. But she deserves better.

Then I realized, the best version of me is *the version of me is the version that never stops getting better* not arbitrary unconstrained ascension, being better *for her*

And that direction isn't obsession or fixation. It's focus. Being better for everyone, or an abstract idea is unconstrained, it's generic, it's unbounded and hard to measure. But being able to say "will this make her life next to me smoother, happier, more loving, or otherwise allow me to love her more wholly?" And operate on the specific answer that results from her specific personhood is a game changer.

And the thing is, the narrative is that you're supposed to change/get better for yourself.

But I did. That's what got me here. I'm *the best there is*. What possible point is there to going higher? To make people like me more? Dumb. To meet some arbitrary bar? All the ones I haven't done already are dumb.

I'm enough for me. I'm good. I'm done.

But she deserves more. Not because she deserves more than I do. But because she has different things she wants. And by being focused, I'm not just swallowing the world, I'm improving on purpose towards something I value greatly.

And most importantly, that song is huge, not specifically, but conceptually. Because I don't need to be *less* of any part of me. She likes me as me. But by being more of what she loves, I make it easier to stand next to me. Easier to talk to me. Easier to understand me.

And because she is, as I've mentioned, the kind of person I like best, these initiatives aren't just towards her, they put me in a place to be easier for my favorite kind of people to be around. And that sounds like a real path to happiness to me.

And if that's not "making me want to be a better person" and "being the best version of myself", I don't know what is

This one is interesting. Because in the first few days of crushing I was vibing with this, because it's a bop, and I love Tessa Violet.

But what I realized, and it might have been why I started the playlist is that this is probably how *she* experiences attraction natively.

Not necessarily every time. But for me this is like a little daydream. But for Tessa, it's very likely a real set of feelings. And as Tessa and my girl are more similar to each other than me, that's probably a fair mapping.

But the daydream part is important. Because this song is *fun* to feel. This song describes a crush, a longing, a sense of unresolvedness that is entirely pleasant.

But it requires distance. In order for this song to be real to her, I have to let her pursue *me*, even and especially if that looks weird to me and is very likely abnormal to her. But if my read on her is correct, it's exactly what she's missing. She knows I'm Apex, that's obvious. But she's kind of the definition of a pursuit object. So, I'm natively the pursuer, she's natively the prize. Flipping it isn't just inversion for its own sake, it's demonstrating something I think is one of the core ways we're compatible. We're both very visible types, so much so that we define those types for those who know us. But we're not just those types, and need to be able to be the less legible versions of ourselves without getting looks from the other. And our genders are not irrelevant here. I'm agender, but identify as a woman if it's relevant, and despite being pan, label myself as a lesbian. And to her, I'm a girl. But between being Apex and being AMAB, it would be easy to collapse our relationship into "cishet with labels", but my labels aren't decorative, I really AM not a man. And if that's true, there's no structural contract for me to pursue, and by leaving this door open for her, I'm showing, as early as possible, that however Apex I may be, I'm not just that shape. And she's also pan. Me being a man isn't necessarily a deal breaker. But as a lesbian, a trans girl who acts like a man when it gets her her way is fucking annoying. This one hits *hard* every time I hear it. Because it feels like being *seen* in such an intimate sideways way that I'm unfamiliar with, but completely nakedly affectionate.

The "face you pull for strangers" and "voice you assume on the phone" thing, I'm historically very sensitive about having things like this pointed out. Because I usually do them on purpose, and I hate people pretending they caught something I'm not aware of. Part of it is trauma about being caught doing things I wasn't aware of, but I'm not going there now.

What's important is that when these landed on me I felt "oh, she's going to see things about me that I didn't do on purpose and form opinions on them", that's being seen in the realest way. And it's not scary because I'm afraid she'll dislike me. It's because I'm afraid she'll like a version of me I don't understand and therefore don't know how to be. I'm less afraid of this than I used to be, but even now, I think it's the inability to be better at something important. But the whole point here is that this little thing is enough. It doesn't need to be fixed or improved. And that's not native to me

Then "not a prize to be won" and "you are the giant teddy bear", to me this says "you're more than your achievements, your spectacle, your capabilities, I'm not looking at you because you glow, I choose different things to like" but also "you are the one I want" and "you are the prize". I've never been the prize, that hits weird for me. And I need to be able to believe it in order to receive it, thus why it's here.

Then "I love that you love Hemingway", damn, this line smacked into me so hard when i heard it the first time. Because I do love Hemingway, I prefer Tolstoy, but I will casually reference "For Whom the Bell Tolls" in conversation because this is the kind of person I am. A wicked smart, very well read one. But the reason this line is here is because girls don't typically love guys who love Hemingway, and for good reason. "Masculine angst" is a term I've heard used, and it maps to some of the guys I know who like Hemingway, who I can't stand. It's their whole personality. And it makes it suffocating to be around them. People like my girl don't get close to these people because everything becomes 90 kinds of intellectual and the conversation gets heavy in ways they don't want. It's not that she's dumb, Hemingway just isn't her style. And so, I already am this kind, I'm wicked smart and read a lot, but I'm very accessible. So this line hit me as "oh, that part too?", not as an aspiration.

And "mountains out of molehills", yeah.... I'm not one well known for proportional responses. This is a very endearing feature of mine if you choose to see it that way, but it's not typically seen that way

Right. That was good. But you missed the last thing I said about Hemingway. I already *am* the right kind here. That's why hearing it here hits. It's being seen for something I see as irrelevant, especially and specifically to her, and loved for it.

And because although my references aren't important to me, I wouldn't spend so much time reading if it wasn't important to me, being loved for this not so easily lovable thing hits hard.
