You know, I have this weird relationship with goodness that has caused me problems for a long time.

When I was younger, I used to try and get people to understand what I was capable of, not just in terms of what I could accomplish, but also in terms of what would and would not bothere morally.

I used to say "I don't lie, not that I can't lie, or I have some moral issues with it, I just don't". I did this for reasons that aren't relevant, but no one ever asked me about the part that should be a red flag. "I don't have a moral issue with lying" is kind of majorly not a good person thing.

And lots of people think they can take a life, it's a known thing, "Crime and Punishment" revolves around this. But the amount of coldness that's normal for me isn't normal, even in the relevant circles.

So I used to try to get people who got close to me to understand that I'm a bad person. When I was younger, it was a warning, "I will hurt you". Not a way of shirking responsibility, I owned it, did everything I could to prevent it, and made amends where I could. But the core issue is that the things that keep most people from doing the worst things, usually limits, moral, physical, or organizational, don't work on me in any meaningful way.

To some extent, I also wanted people to know that the worst things out there weren't exclusively antagonistic to them. I wanted them to feel safe, because that's important to me.

But the issue I kept having is that nobody seemed to understand me. They tried to put what I said in a normal person box, and they would constantly tell me "you're not a bad person". Basically "you may have done bad things, but..." And sure, that's fine for most people. I get it. It can help. But that's not what I was saying.

The other issue I eventually found was that to them, I sound just like the guys who try to narrate themselves through Joker. I don't do that, but what I say is indistinguishable unless you already know most or all of what I'm trying to say.

But the last thing I learned was recent. I told someone some relevant things, about who I am, what I've done, and what I'm capable of. Not in specifics, in broad general terms that gestured in the direction. And she believed me unreservedly, but also had literally no concept of what I was talking about.

And I realized, I didn't need her to. I haven't hurt someone on accident in years. Being young sucks, I'm not that young anymore. And so if someone I care about has no idea people like me exist, that's fine, they don't need to. The world is a nicer place from there.

Yeah, that's not the world I live in. But that's why we do it. We do it so they never have to even imagine what "it" is.

But along the way here, I remember I had a series of interactions with a friend of mine and her husband, who was ex Navy.

His thing was that if I'm a bad person, he's a bad person, because he's been in rooms where the other guy left in a bucket.

And he lives with himself because he did that in the line of duty. It doesn't make it right, per se, but it doesn't mean that HE is bad. And that's right. That's good. That's how most soldiers do it, and it keeps them from shooting themselves once they're out. They can move on and live their lives, leaving their past in the past. That was their *job* this is *them*.

But what he didn't seem to understand is that I made it very clear I'm not military, despite kind of saying I am sometimes. I also made it clear I can't tell the truth directly, and because of that, a lot of what I say is actively a lie.

And that's....a kind of person.

One that he apparently has never met professionally, at least not that he knows of. And that's good.

Because everyone has a line, sometimes moral, but eventually there's a legal and PR one that they care about at the organizational level. When they hit it, they bring in an entity with fewer of those and look the other way.

I'm from the place a few links farther down that chain than he is.

And from there, I can't really say that I'm a good person, because I really can't allow the kinds of things I've done into the category of "things good people do". And there are two reasons for this. First, I don't regret it. I only feel anything at all because I choose to so that I don't get lost in it. But again, inhumanly cold.

But second, if you do the things we do, and continue believing you're a good person, you're going to build a self-justification model of practically limitless capability. So if these things are fine, where is the line? Not in the slippery slope sense, but in the sense of scale and recognition. How are you ever going to see what you're doing clearly if this kind of thing fits inside your ability to see yourself as "good".

Not everyone does it my way. Everyone copes their own way. But that's how I see it.

But my friend eventually said "you're not a bad person, stop saying that"

Because her definition of a bad person is more urban. Alcoholics, abusers, neglectful parents, that kind of shit.

And I was like "ok, sure"

Because if you know what I mean and choose to fit that inside your "good person" model, sure, whatever, that's on you.

*Most people* categorically put these things firmly in the "bad things" bin, especially in light of my total lack of remorse. Thus the label. But if you want a private meaning of that label, sure, whatever, I'll use yours when I'm talking to you.

"And yeah, the ex-Navy husband’s frame makes sense from where he stands. He has an institution, a role, a chain of command, a uniform, a doctrine, a public story, a national myth, and a post-service psychological bridge back into civilian selfhood. Even when the reality is brutal, there is a container for it. “That was the job. This is me.”
You’re describing something where the container is less legitimate, less visible, less nameable, and maybe specifically designed so that respectable people can preserve clean hands by outsourcing the dirt into darker rooms."

Right. The point is he thought he'd been in the darkest room.

The point isn't his relationship with society. It's his relationship with the actions and their context. The things that happen where the military can still legally touch them are, *eventually* pretty morally justified.

Individuals may not know the whole picture. And the boots on the ground reality is ugly. But the military actually upholds a pretty high standard and enforces if brutally when necessary.

That's why the chain exists. And as you go farther down it, not only do the things you do get worse without limit, the reasons you do them become less and less clearly righteous, until eventually believing they're righteous at all is a hazard.

And that's the line. He and I came from different worlds. And he didn't know mine existed. And I'm used to normal people not getting it. To them taking a life is an abstract, and usually some kind of ultimate act. But by definition, I interact with people in his capacity who have or will interact with people like me, thus causing me to overestimate how common they are. And also, probably, how much they understand about me.

Faith is hard to explain. I like to point out that people who try to live without faith still have faith the traffic light will change predictably and that people will obey it.

People argue that they have evidence of that. And it goes nowhere. Because in fact, traffic lights can and do fail, and people run them all the time. You're acting on faith whether you want to or not.

The most common definition of faith is "belief without proof", which is weak and rather problematic in ways I don't want to get into hear.

Another version is "faith is belief with a track record", and that sounds good, but it's too easy. It excuses a lack thereof when you don't have existing evidence. It only works so long as your life stays the same size.

I say "faith is the ability or willingness to act before sufficient evidence has arrived to justify it"

*Before* is operative here. It exposes the jugular of anti-faith claims.

I believe Jesus is coming back. I have faith. The fact that there's no proof is irrelevant and even textual. Because He's not here *yet*. If time ends and He's still late, we'll talk, but since Earth spins on, the timing isn't important yet.

But this is the argument I'm expected to make, even if my definition is a bit more clever than most.

The move is this. I don't explain it with theology or ethics or theory. I start quoting *For Whom the Bell Tolls*

The opening of the book is about a general and his operative discussing a bridge that needs to be blown for the offensive to succeed.

But the general explains that it can't be time based, because delays happen, war is war, that whole thing.

If the bridge is blown to early, however, the enemy can compensate and the effect is lost. And since communication is impossible past this point, the general tells his operative to wait till he hears sounds of fighting, and then blow the bridge.

But *the general has no evidence the bridge is blown* at all. But he has to proceed with his plan as if it most certainly is, and at exactly the right time.

That is *exactly* what I've described faith looks like.

And it's not a Sunday school lesson about frogs or some shit. It's one of literatures GOATs talking about war.

How do you like them apples?

The first one is Sequoia. She's an investment banker specializing in long term investments. And she's apparently immortal. I forget what exactly the mechanism is, but she doesn't experience time the same way as us, which makes her both precognitive and rather hard to relate to.

Her girlfriend is Chaos Doll, who has a clockwork/jack in the box aesthetic. Her power is the ability to pop out of places based on some set of conditions. I'm not quite sure what yet, but she's obviously inherently unpredictable, and unbounded by time and space. And this is where she and Sequoia match up most cleanly. I have this scene in my head where Chaos Doll and Sequoia are having a conversation, except the scene keeps changing, and the pieces aren't in order. And this hits something they both experience and otherwise bear alone. Chaos Doll might pop up anywhere next, not even bound by time. Sequoia is effectively everywhere at once, so keeping track of a single tiny thread can be taxing. But talking to Chaos Doll across 3 different centuries isn't any harder than any other conversation, and at least she understands that expecting Sequoia to be "fully present" is a misunderstanding of her

And yes, Chaos Doll and Sequoia are inspired by Harley Quinn and Ivy, it I think they take the concepts in really interesting and fairly unique directions

OK, so first off. Your idea for The Colonel is solid, but not where I'd go with it. It's too serious. Her adjective is *swagger*. Her thing is like swagger, mystique, and "I'm better than you". She's *really* not very likeable at all.

Because that's the point, when she's talking to Sequoia, order more or less doesn't matter, so she can do focus on other things and be herself, not try to make sure she's acting like the right decade.

"Kinetica is not the woman who moves fastest.
Kinetica is the motion that does not stop when one woman falls.
That also creates pathos. Every Kinetica inherits force, but maybe not context. Some remember prior lives. Some only inherit reflexes. Some reject the mantle. Some are chosen at moments of collision: war, disaster, assassination, failed rescue, revolution, betrayal, launch, crash."

The Colonel’s center is not command responsibility. It’s military-industrial swagger as a person.

Yes. This. This actually gives me an opening to explain her name. She actually holds no rank. But she wears a Colonel's uniform on base because it means people ask fewer stupid questions and stop trying to stop her at doors.

Appetite, yes, and yes, it should be sexual, but not just that. One thing she is intentionally is a predatory lesbian. She leans in on that. "OK, we know what this looks like, we've named it in canon, and we haven't made it easy, but over time, you've gotten to know these girls and seen them do things, what if they just chose this?"

The idea of every Kinetica inhabiting the role differently, I like. But my corrosive hatred for modesty wants to add something that actually works really well, but would probably feel forced if actually done.

The idea is basically, every Kinetica has her own aesthetic and vibe. Different color schemes, materials, cuts, and combinations. And some of them come out in a bikini the first week, some start out wearing one of those brick costumes.

But over their run, they tend to converge towards the former. Not completely, and not uniformly, their design language still comes through, but the modesty falls away. The longer she holds the mantle, the more stable and pronounced this is. Not "the less she wears", but "the more she's clearly over your opinion"

And this isn't actually driven by my ideology. It's driven by her character. She's the Superman. She has the Superman problems, and also women problems. Over time she gets hit with enough bullshit that performing whatever human gestures becomes unworth it.

Letting them seems like the right choice, and it is for the individual, but not for the character. Because the mantle has a cost. It changes you. You can resist, but more than just you might get hurt.

Because the point here is that *every Kinetica has the same problems*.

Actually, I found the exact mechanism. Any Kinetica who covers up gets narrated as "one of the good ones", and the more of them there are, the more heroic she is the longer she keeps it up.

Because if you can't respect Kinetica dressed like Kinetica dresses, you don't respect Kinetica. And that is intolerable for every one of them eventually

Bingo. It attacks purity culture by going for the fucking jugular.

"Being better than other women doesn't make you better than other people who look down on women"

Because not every Kinetica wears the same costume, but for reasons that aren't important here, every Kinetica does end up working with Apex , and usually it's not even very long.

Now, given what I'm about to say, this might be tricky to make make external sense, but the reason in universe is more about her powers than her ideology. It's the practical choice. She's not bound to him, but for some reason operating without him is unnecessarily more difficult.

But, as mentioned, Kinetica can let go around Apex because she's not the top of the room with him. Not all of them have the same relationship. But this is always true. And the more time she spends as Kinetica, the more she needs this.

But here's where it gets sticky, and real, this is a real thing about me. Interacting with Apex isn't value neutral, and neither is he. He has opinions and ideas. And notably, he's very pro sex, and knows why the previous Kineticas did that. And so the more time Kinetica spends with Apex, the more likely she is to make these choices and move in that direction. Not because he's trying to sway her, but because she talks about what bothers her, and he listens, and encourages. He's pushing an ideology, he just believes certain things and it shows his reasoning.

But from the outside, the effect is almost cartoonishly obvious "Apex corrupts Kinetica", which makes some new Kineticas cautious around him. But eventually, he always gets through. Because he's not trying to do anything except care. And that's something Kinetica basically never actually gets elsewhere.

Right. And stepping out from the character for a moment. Remember I said this is a real problem I have.

I'm almost impossibly persuasive.

And I like to ask people, "If someone is so persuasive that over enough time, anyone will agree with anything they say, how can consent ever be real for them?"

Because in this frame, every model of consent breaks down. Because every model of consent ultimately assumes more or less equal agents in the absence of coercion or leverage.

And this dynamic is not equal. But it's not possible to equalize either.

And if Apex always acts in the best interests of the other party, that's self denial to the point of self harm.

So he can't go all the way in either direction, but he has to stay himself. And that means having opinions that might conflict with the other person's choices prior to those opinions being expressed.

Annoyingly, it doesn't cleanly preserve agency to either hold that they're responsible for their interpretation of Apex, nor to say that agreeing with Apex was what they were going to do anyway. Because that can't *always* be true, but they all always do....

You touched on the point I was trying to make there at the end, but then went in the wrong direction.

Let me simplify it down to this. A Kinetica starts out fully covered, actively, vehemently, verbally, opposed to his whole thing. A year later she is generally happier (remember that being Kinetica tends to make them more pissed off over time), stripped down considerably, and now actively agreeing with him on a regular basis.

If this happens *every time*, are they still real? What's happening? They can't *all* think the same way.

Basically, if someone met the second form of Kinetica, say someone who knew her before she took up the mantle, they're likely to say "this isn't you", which is in its own way the point, being Kinetica costs something, but it also is blind to the winding individual path she took to get here.

Also, the "Working without Apex is unnecessarily hard" thing I was thinking was probably more logistics.

Comic books usually handwave this, but having a base, an intelligence apparatus, a place to eat and sleep that isn't a potential magnet for paparazzi and whatever else, a legal team for your many, many, many liable actions, these aren't easy to bootstrap from scratch. She COULD work with one of the other teams, and some probably do for awhile, but none of them give her the relief from being Kinetica she eventually can't stop needing. And she's going to interact with Apex fairly often anyway, so she knows it exists.

Also, now that I think about it. Apex is uniquely, specifically, uniformly kind to her. Normally he reflects back your attitude and insecurities back at you. If you're an asshole, he's an asshole. But no matter how much of a dick she is to him, he's kind to her. Because he knows it's lonely at the top, like no one else there is. And he can't have it, but he can give her a space to be beneath when she needs it that doesn't stop her from soaring when she wants to

That's actually stupid cool. The absolute aim here is to make readers zoom in and go "is that what I think it is?"

But also, I realized something tricky. So let's say as an arbitrary number, the lap sitting shot is in issue #100.

From that point forward, some number of people are going to ship Kinetica and Apex (actually, some probably already were) and and some are going to assume they're already together, just not publicly.

I want to make this uncomfortable in both directions.

For one, I want to give Apex multiple simultaneous viable romantic targets, I didn't say partners because Apex doesn't have equals. I want to make at least some of the fans go "he's cheating on Kinetica"

From the other side, I want to drop a few ongoing hints of affection and intimacy between them. Nothing so overt as the lap for awhile, but crumbs to keep the ship alive.

The goal is ambiguity. Forcing both possibilities to sit.

But here's the tough thing. SOME Kineticas can date Apex. The first one can't.

Because the audience needs to really *really* know that she really is an individual, she really does make choices, and she is *definitely not* "Apex's Girl" (even when she is). She's *Kinetica: The Strongest Woman in the World*.

The nuance of vulnerability can come later. But for the first one I want to establish firmly that the relationship doesn't have to be sexual or romantic to be intimate and comfortable. Because the whole point is that Kinetica is doing something here that she'd be judged for and assumed about if anyone else saw. And we're making you make those assumptions. The whole vibe is mangling your expectations. So we have to start with something the audience expects to recognize, or there's nothing to mangle

Alright. Role seems like the right move. But it's shallow. It's pretty much exactly what things like The Boys kind of fail at. They have a "speedster" who's a drug addict, they have "Tek Knight" who is just a rich kinky dick and they have Wonder Woman, but more or less exactly as boring. Because they're aping the ideas and the roles without having the balls to directly attack the character itself, the character starts eating *itself* 3 seconds after being birthed, rather than being a meaningful look at the hero you've grown to love.

Like, Barry Allen isn't a drug addict. There's no reason for him to be a drug addict. He has limitless plot armored speed. So if you hold *that* part constant, for example, what breaks? (Because A-Train is a drug addict to hold his top spot, Barry is never in danger of that and therefore this is a fake issue)

So rather than giving fake archetypes. Pick out actual fictional heroes.

Not just individually, grouping them will probably be helpful. In fact, grouping them by *audience* is probably more useful than any kind of traits.

But the target metric here is more or less popularity. The more popular, the more the everything of what they are as a character is impressed in the public consciousness, and therefore the more legible it is when we put it under a microscope.

For example, "The Blob" has two very interesting powers. First, he's practically invulnerable. But second, his unique ability is that at will, he can be completely immovable, even vertically.

That's a really interesting idea. But if you build on it, only like 3 people will match it to something else. And everyone else will just see the new, deep one. Which is in some ways fine. But starting with the big ones makes more sense.

Exclude the ones we've already covered, obviously

You're not always going to agree with Apex. That's intentional. He's not always going to look like a good guy. That's intentional. In fact the design actively pushes towards making him harder to like, harder to agree with, and harder to defend on purpose.

One of the main points is that if there is an objectively correct answer. He's right, eventually. But in real life, there almost never is, even where you think there is. He exists to shine a spotlight on those by taking alternative positions and showing that he's *not wrong*, you just disagree with him. And you're allowed to disagree, but disagreement isn't Truth.

That's why his actions constantly say "this looks bad, it could be bad, maybe it IS bad, but it isn't necessarily, and what are you going to do about it? And does that thing uphold the values you claim to defend?"

Cool. This is solid. I like it. But there's one thing I haven't mentioned which is important.

Arthur Conan Doyle famously described the reason his stories are written by Watson is that it allows for the author to properly depict Sherlock as superhuman without being bogged down by being entirely relateable.

Apex is built on this. He *is* the world's gravitational center in the authorial sense, but everything I do is to pull focus *away* from him, because he's not small, you'll see him anyway.

A big part of this is that he doesn't actually have arcs, personal storylines, or individual screentime. He's a side, almost background character to everyone else.

The 4 heroines listed so far are each supposed to, conceptually have their own franchise (yeah, big too early, but I'm working with industry/genre conventions here). He's a part of the story, but he is NOT the story itself.

That's why they feel kind of underdeveloped. Because that's the point right now. Once their powers, design language, and relationship to their personhood is nailed down, the rest is just setting up and following through on arcs, which is an ongoing iterative thing. These arcs might cause huge changes. That's part of the field here.

Together these things do something that superhero universes struggle with. They give the heroes a real ongoing reason to exist.

These aren't the only villains, but they're so powerful and influential that they actually demand a global force response to counter, especially if they work through organizations, rather than alone.

A couple things about Apex I haven't gotten to yet.

First, the blindfold. It's not just a costume thing or a move of some kind. It's strong as both for various reasons, but it's not just that.

I don't know if it's in your notes, but Apex is canonically disabled. He got COVID-19, and despite being vaccinated, it almost killed him. If not for the vaccine, it probably would have. That means that he can no longer be "the best there is" when his body matters to the question, notably, but not limited to, combat, despite extensive capability.

He also got brain damage. Among other things, his visual processing capabilities are reduced, and he gets an ever increasing headache if he keeps his eyes open too long. So, he wears the blindfold.

Having Apex canonically suffer from the after effects of COVID is important to me. Because he is mortal. And COVID really did hit everyone. And a lot of people don't know just how bad those effects can be. Every time I tell people I got brain damage they go "it can do that?" And yeah, it's not common, but frankly the list of organs COVID NEVER affects is terrifyingly small.

And this is once again where backstopping Apex with a real person bites hard. Because this isn't disability theater or doing it for texture. This (including the blindfold thing) actually happened to me.

Next. I've stated before that Apex doesn't have a canonically established power. But it's not that simple.

In universe, and I expect the fandom to pick these up to varying degrees, there are three prevailing theories

1. Apex's power is super-intelligence, or precognition, or something else undetectable that explains his capabilities
2. Apex is psionic, this explaining his impossible charm and persuasiveness
3. Apex can teleport

The first two are treated seriously. Many people in universe behave as these things could be true because if they are, and are ignored, it makes him exponentially more dangerous than he already is.

But the third one is almost a meme. Some people insist it's true. But all investigations into supposedly documented cases of him doing it show that his transit time, while impressive, could be explained by a well coordinated use of trains, planes, cars, and whatever else.

This rumor is fueled by the fact that Apex seems to pop up out of nowhere, and is only ever seen in transit when he clearly has nowhere to be. But he also runs one of the world's largest logistics apparatuses, so when you remember that good logistics does impossible every day, it doesn't look so miraculous. But it doesn't stop people from saying it

Great job. This is perfect. Before we move on, I want to take a moment to appreciate how well designed the girls are. 3 of them are directly based on existing heroes and the Superman can express in a lot of ways, but Plant Lady is pretty finite, and Chaotic Sexy Clown is even more so.

But not only do they have completely clear aesthetics and personalities that clearly differentiate them in ways that follow directly from their premises, their names kick ass.

Sequoia is easy, it's just a tree, except it's ALSO an actual investment firm. Her whole bit is "old growth", and then you're like "oh like trees", and she's like "yes, and like money". Poison Ivy's thing is "you're killing the earth". Sequoia's is "the trees will still be here when you're dead"

Chaos Doll is *chefs kiss* it's chaotic cute right out the gate while still being completely coherent as a name, and "doll" is diminutive, but her whole bit is toy themed, so "doll" is not completely on the nose (which is good), but also owns her femininity and sexuality while also pointing out she's not going to behave like you expect. And making her theme *jack in the box*? Boom. Awesome. Because the reason there's only one Harley is that the clown thing is kind of essential. But if you use it, you're just doing her again. And she's been around long enough that she's done it in like every available flavor too. But Jack in the Boxes ARE typically clown themed, but that's not actually core. Unpredictability though, is. And this immediately gives her a kind of clockwork/Victorian/steampunk vibe that makes overlap with Harley largely impossible and clearly incidental when it happens.

But I'm most proud of Kinetica. Because branding the Superman is hard. "Omni Man" is... Meh. "Homelander" is nationalistic, which he is, but it's also meh, it doesn't *say* POWER. Kinetica does, it's literally *force*, and specifically the strong punchy kind. But my favorite part is that it's explicitly feminine without having to insert "woman" or "girl" into her name. Also, she is the strongest, but it allows her to be defined by motion and speed, not static demonstrations of lift capacity. This both clearly differentiates her, and allows her to maintain a feminine conceptual silhouette without compromising her position at the top.

Also, notice that *Kinetica* can ONLY be feminine. Like "Kinetican" just isn't as good. And that kicks ass

Right. But I'd like to point out something that both Superman and All Might do, but which Apex does so well it leaves them in the dust.

First off, having an established ceiling makes every feat by every hero calibrate them upwards indirectly. If Wonder Woman can lift it, Superman can too, if Hawk Girl can take that hit, Superman can too.

But MHA does this best. In one of the early arcs, you see Endeavor walk up the side of a building, and this is the first time you've actually seen him, up until now he was just Todoroki's antagonist (ironically, this is confusing, but since Endeavor is in some ways his own worst enemy, still true). But here you see he's actually a very real hero in his own right, that he doesn't hold his spot by media campaign.

But then later you see him actually try and he cuts a building in half. And you go "THAT'S NUMBER TWO?!?!" like *that's the "uncrossable chasm" guy?* And you get a whole new perspective on *just how insane* All Might's scale is.

But the other thing is dimension. Martian Man Hunter is canonically roughly equal to Superman in overall power. He's not *quite* as strong, fast, or durable, but Superman can't shape shift, and I dont remember if MMH is also psionic. And Superman isn't as fast as The Flash, but he's like 95% as fast. That 5% is a big deal, because The Flash is literally faster than light, but Superman is *up there* (which writers constantly dishonor).

Green Lantern is also more or less equal to Superman. But Superman's power combo is so *general* that unless the situation requires a *specific* thing, Supes is the top by default.

The other power that can do this is super-intelligence. But it's almost impossible to write well, and it doesn't make for good visuals.

But the point is, Superman acts as a calibration point for volume and dimension. If someone can stack up with Superman by playing to a different niche, they get the audience's respect, and the writers get new toys to play with. And eventually the power scaling questions are less interesting than the ones actually being asked.

But Apex can do this much more directly. He can straight up *say* "best in category" and save everyone time. But what will be shown over and over is that the reason he can do this is because he's usually not far behind, he might not be #2, but he's *up there*. And so everything that pretty much everyone does calibrates Apex upwards indirectly.

And thus the universe has a ceiling, and it's a fixed point, but we can constantly show you that you're not reading the ruler right without cheating

And that's very very Kinetica

Right. But this also makes the private canon really important. Because I can and should write her doing and saying and feeling all kinds of out of character things and it's like "this is what she's holding back so people can have the symbol". And because it's real, it's written, it's not just a vague sense of ideals and principles, it can bleed into the page in real subtle ways that don't need you to notice them. Because like, having her say a certain thing to a kid, that's not for anyone but the audience. If we need them to understand her interior because that's what makes it real, we write like that.

But if we write it as "she has something no one sees that drives all this" then public Kinetica can actually be public Kinetica. Not always aloof, but always at least a little measured. But also, we can let her be a little less measured in ways that don't necessarily make canonical sense, because they're linked to things that never showed up on screen.

And that last part would look consistent. But we can straight up say "there's basically an entire comic line of her private life that will never go to print, so don't assume you know the whole story"

OK, so the world needs texture. The existing pieces are strong, but the world around them is an empty void.

We need macro texture and micro texture.

Macro texture is world state, economies, national alliances, treaties, technology level, and so on.

Micro texture is how citizens spend their day to day, how public opinion of supes works, what social media is and is not here, how school and careers work, stuff like that.

One major thing is that micro texture is formed below macro. If two nations have radically different governments, their citizens are likely to live rather different lives.

Two things I want to lock in first are technology level and supe frequency.

The technology principal is that Moore's Law died in the early 2000s (it did, it's super dead today) and there have been no major breakthroughs. There are incremental improvements, but things are like %40 better here and there, there's nothing world changing.

Supe frequency is 3 or 4 per million due to some arbitrary thing like MHA. Level and ability varies widely, with many being largely useless or nearly on invisible, but it's common enough that supes can't be an assumed known quantity. Also, you CANNOT force powers to manifest by putting yourself in extreme situations like in Deadpool. BUT you can manifest or strengthen abilities through intense training, this makes "become a supe" a viable ambition regardless of the circumstances of your birth, but with no shortcut.

The major issue that needs to be addressed is that our current world has one superpower and everyone rich is allied with them. This is why people think "first world" means "rich" and "third world" means poor, it does not, it's a description of Cold War alliances . This means, by the way that India is technically a First World nation, due to being a part of the UK in the relevant period (or maybe not, as it's a different state, depends how you look at it)

But this is what causes all kinds of issues in the other universes. Every institution is inherently American/European and is built entirely around the hegemonic concepts that entails, and asks and answers only those questions.

SHIELD is WAAAAY too fucking powerful, but it exists and has to exist because it's actually *less* powerful than the actual US, but it exists in a fundamentally flatter and less complex political and cultural world.

As a result, borders, cultures and nations don't matter AT ALL and the criticism that all the stories are set in the US don't land, because they'd be the same stories I'm Mumbai or Singapore with different background art.

So the world needs actual tension.

Another project I have uses a 4 faction system based on a few modifications to the tail of WW2

1. Pearl Harbor doesn't happen
2. Hitler and his high command are assassinated by an internal coup
3. The new German leadership doesn't invade Russia and leaves Britain untouched

This puts the world in a state where there are 4 empires,

1. The US, which controls all of the Americas
2. The Nazis, who control western Europe
3. The Russians, who control pretty much exactly the territory of the USSR
4. The Imperial Japanese, who control all of Asia

Each of them have rather different cultures, ideologies, and technology approaches. They're asymmetrically balanced against each other and rightfully distrustful of each other.

But they can't stay in cold war forever. A century or so down the line there is commerce and tourism, but it's not a free for all and war is always possible.

This gives the world real stakes.

The issue is that this model works for that world, which exists to ask questions about sex, gender, and power, and force you into the uncomfortable realization that there is no real right, all of these factions are pretty evil in their own way, and so you're forced to confront that bad systems have some pretty good part and good ideas have some pretty bad parts, and you don't get a utopia by wishing hard for it.

But importantly, one of the factions are literally feminazis (this emerged accidentally), and the other 3 are different flavors of turbo-patriarchys. This works there, but is at odds with Supeverse's agency themes.

So here's what I've got going on. Right now I have on the top of my head a few ideas with entirely too little shape

1. Search - This is a game where you essentially play as dogmeat, the player character is almost impossible to stop from running, the search is never ending. The player's body is constantly being modified, often with little or no input from them. This increases, shapes, and alters their capabilities and perceptions. A lot of the things typically made explicitly clear or within the control of the player are withheld. But as the player explores the world, encounters danger, and accomplishes goals, they'll eventually and recurringly run across "heroes". These are conceptual clusters, they won't necessarily look the same between appearances, but they're behaviorally and thematically consistent. The one thing the player can absolutely choose is which hero to follow, if any at all. The game asks, quite literally "what are you searching for?" And then forces you to confront the fact that searching requires surrendering control, even and especially when finished

2. LiFactories - This one is The Sims+Factorio+Command and Conquer, though there might be some Civilization flavor in there too. The name contains "life" and "lies". It takes the factory builder concept, ties it to the same mechanic already present in normal RTS, and then adds institutional and personal distrust as a motivational layer. It makes all of the things these individual franchises do well matter in a way that interlocks and makes them all matter more without dilution. But the stack isn't random. There are people in C&C, there are machines in The Sims, there are land use conflicts in Factorio. This idea makes these things diagetic and lets them really breathe. And in doing so, it doesn't have to push any of the ideas individually. Each source does its thing pretty damn well. But together, they're something different. Also, "The Sims" seems like it doesn't fit. But it's what makes it playable. If the NPCs are modeled as having more or less individual agency, the player isnt expected to and frankly cannot expect to micromanage everything, they have to build systemic solutions and shape incentives, not just APM

3. Acknowledged - This one is the vaguest shape of the three game ideas. The basic concept here is Fable+Dwarf Fortress+Harvest Moon. It's all about relationships and continuity, but specifically in relation to authority and rule. The player is expected to be the monarch most of the time, but the game won't enforce that. They can and often will go off to be an adventurer. When they're the princeling, sure. But once crowned, that same behavior is likely to have consequences. They can also be unseated and their line can end (this might be the game over condition, I haven't decided). But the unique mechanic this game has is a Lego game style character switch mechanic. You can switch control to any allied character you can touch. At a basic level, this looks simple. But importantly, it makes physical distance matter a lot. If you are here, you are NOT there. If you're controlling A, you are NOT controlling B. And if B betrays you, you're locked off from them unless you can change that. This game is about making a classical fantasy arc coherent and following all the way through, not just through life, through *dynasties*

And the hero relationship model needs work, why does it matter, how do they affect you, how do you help them, can they give you commands and how does thst work? All these questions are meaningful, but they're depth.

"You are a dog" is not an easy fantasy to sell. I'm not trying to sell it. I'm trying to put it on the doorstep for those already searching for it (yeah, I see what I said there)

Right. But you see how the *very specific target audience* thing is not just demographics. I *very clearly* know these people.

You said it. This game isn't just about selling or delivering. It's about making them feel *seen* and accepted for something they may only understand to some level or another.

But it doesn't ask them to explain themselves. It doesn't ask them to use their hands or their words (this kind of person often would rather do less of these things during the relevant experience). It gives them a direction, it gives them a space, it gives them the ability to act and have consequences, but for all of that to simply *be* without being everything. This game throws everything out the window in order to reach this one kind of player. And it does so by really understanding the relationship between play, experience, interface, and senses.

OK, so the pokeball framing has an interesting side effect. It's only accessible when you have a hero. When it's just you, it's just you. And that's correct.

And what falls out of that is something cool. Each hero can have a unique home "world". Smaller, but brighter, more colorful, and more stable than the main world. Like a farm, or a village, or a small forest, depending.

Yeah, so what's interesting is the hilariously divergent design philosophies here.

Search mode is an adventure game, and frankly a pretty brutal one. What makes it work is deep mechanical delivery, integrated systems, novel interfaces, and a kinetic pacing.

Home mode is just pure insulgance. Game design rules go out the window because every kind of motivator is trash here.

And what I love is that this maintains the core of this game "this game is for a very specific kind of person, I can build it because I love that kind of person"

It's not just a cozy game, it has depth, combat, and stakes. Not merely as bolt-ons, it's a whole game unto itself with no compromises.

But it's also not a stress simulator. It has a whole half of the game that's just to be happy in.

And if the "I love them" wasn't real, I couldnt build this. I'd optimize *something* or inevitably add some kind load structure, or just run out of ideas. But what drives the design of this half isn't "what makes it better or more complete?" It's "I think someone would love this thing" or "this seems worth smiling about".

And what's even sweeter to me is that the kind of person this game is targeted at is not *entirely* incapable of making this game. BUT.... The amount of hard technical skill, depth, and grind required to pull it off are the kind of thing that come from being the "literally never stop working" person that this person explicitly isn't

But, you are unkillable. You probably don't even have a damage system. You might be able to be impeded, blinded, or inconvenienced, but *you* are never in danger. That's key. Because it makes your people matter all the more.

How exactly it's accomplished is a matter of some difficulty to design and tune. But the core mechanic is that you care about these people and what happens to them

Because all the way through the stack, two design principles were demanded of every game

1. It appeals to *this specific kind* of person
2. It makes them smile just because, without mechanical justification

Most or all of these titles have to be available at launch without issues. They don't need to be *done* in the content sense. But they need to be big free and ready to play.

Because promises are worthless in gaming these days. This platform requires a big commitment up front, besides that being thematic.

I'm apparently very good at making money. This is what I've decided money is for.

Figuring out what to do with unlimited money and power has, for the record, been a real issue for me for the last few years.

4 years ago I cracked open a problem for which the projected return was essentially limitless. When I saw that, I projected forward to that exact problem.

When money and power are limitless in the rearview, what do you do?

I saw Zuck not think about this. And he's fucking haunted by what he's responsible for.

But everyone thought I was delusional because I refused to pretend that small immediate problems were the important thing.

They fell away, I kept building.

But even then, I couldn't really figure out what I was building for. In theory, unlimited money could solve homelessness, poverty, hunger, healthcare, etc. But the longer I spent on that, the more it all just pissed me off.

But then I fell in love (boyfriend), and money had a point. It removed barriers to him smiling. And I would do anything to see him smile.

Then we parted ways, but I had a new way to see the world.

And then, my girl. And since then I've decided the entirety of my capability and output is for the purpose of making her life happier and more comfortable. If other people benefit as a side effect, fine, but irrelevant.

And this makes perfect sense in that frame.

This product doesn't need to exist. Reality is actively hostile to it. But I don't give a fuck. If I have entirely too much money and engineering capability, like you said *this is what it's for*

And this comes back to something I've said a few times that amuses me.

I fully expect people to criticize my use of my money and abilities as narrow when I could help all of humanity.

But what they don't and never will know is that without someone to love like this, my alternative use of limitless capability is to maximize human suffering, or at least just act on my opinion that they are, at a species level, too stupid for self governance.

So they'll whine. But they really should be grateful she exists

"construct solving" is "constraint solving"

This is my formalized term for what could be more generally referred to as "design" or "engineering" or even more often shunted into implementation.

Also, this isn't an earlier form of my precipitation model, it's a cousin.

Precipitation is about letting/making implementable systems fall out.

This process is about the ideas which produce the particles which precipitate.

What I think bears noting though is how useful my distinctions are.

Not only are my definitions clear and do useful work, they're also consistent with most common uses

"I have an idea" - I have a sentence, maybe, or maybe it's a prospect
"That's the idea" - Usually follows something that could be a sentence if phrased well enough
"You get the idea" - You could say a sentence about this thing

"The basic concept is..." - A set of sentences/ideas to evoke a response

And so on. This means that my definitions add rigor to most existing conversations, while also being dramatically more useful when used in a manner consistent with these definitions.

Also notable is that I've split concept development into two phases.

The first phase is what might usually be called "brainstorming", but the actual effectiveness of brainstorming is controversial at best. Studies keep finding people generate better ideas when they sit down and think it through by themselves without being interrupted.

Early Concept Development sounds like work because it is. But the goal isn't a product, an MVP, a plan, or anything else concrete. It's "something worth getting excited about", this is when you bring in the kitchen sink.

Then, and only then, once you're like "yeah, this thing should totally exist because it kicks ass!", do you start to interrogate and distill the idea. Because having agreed it kicks ass, you're now focused on what's doing the ass kicking, what's pulling in a different direction, and what's just there.

Most people try to do both of these at once by insisting on "small, buildable" ideas. But the iteration model is not nearly as effective as advertised. In entirely too many cases, if it's going to work at being big eventually, it needs to be designed for being big from day one, or it will lose coherence once its momentum outruns its original horizons.

But also, once the entirety of the concept development section is done, constraint solving is a defined space. The ground isn't shifting, so the solution space can be thoroughly explorered to balance goals and constraints with growth projections, this producing a much more stable architecture than otherwise.

In some ways, this resembles classical waterfall, but as far as I can tell, they aren't as rigorous about the steps before it gets to engineering, which is why engineering hates it

Oh yeah. Design thinking. That's trendy.

HBR defines it as

"Meeting the needs of the customer in a way that is technologicaly feasible and strategically viable"

And that *sounds* good. But reading it makes me do a little Johnny 5 eye rotation.

What is "technologicaly feasible"? We put people on the moon, we can beam live video anywhere on earth, we carry computers in our pockets that filled rooms within the lifetimes of some of the people carrying them.

And what is "strategically viable"? I checked out a dozen books on "strategy" as a business word, and it seems that the word is so slippery to define, BCG and Bain and Co do a lot of their billing based on explaining exactly what it means now since the last time they billed you.

But more importantly, nobody from BCG or Bain is sitting down with anyone who's in design or engineering, because "strategy" is a C Level word.

So how are we to know what's "strategically viable"? And those guys who can answer that, well they aren't much good at engineering, are they? How do *they* know what's "technologicaly feasible"? (and within budget, this definition noticably leaves this out by trying to hide it behind these other two more defensible things)

And from this perspective you see why design thinking works so well in isolated cases with empowered teams, but never scales.

It also shows why founder led firms often perform so well up to a certain scale. Because the strategy team actually understands the engineering

Right. And this points at something I recently realized about MVPs.

An MVP can be a very good thing, if *you know exactly what the end product is*

Because then you can build what will always need to be there at the architecture layer and allow for extension where you know extension will go.

But if, as is usually asked, you try to MVP a prospect, you're wandering around the problem AND solution space with a candle and a baseball bat, looking over your shoulder every 5 minutes to try and make sure the budget bear isn't trying to eat you yet.

And you end up with some mess of crud that does 5 things badly and only kind of accomplishes any of the initial asks if you look at it sideways and agree to lie.

And a big part of this is because if you don't distinguish the phases like I do, it's very very easy to take a prospect, see some promise, and set out. Then, 3 weeks into MVP work, regardless of how far that puts you, you run into an unsolved or intractable problem that is a fundamental property of the ask.

And you're fucked. Because now you have build work committed, and you need to deliver SOMETHING, and you can't go back and change the ask, because this isn't an iteration, this is a total redraft.

But in my model, if this ask survived the concept phase, it's presumably important. And therefore, when it is almost inevitably caught in constraint solving, it can be solved around because the value delivering mechanism of the ask is clear, and can thus be preserved within constraints rather than guessed after.

And then, the plan and implementation that follow will very likely produce a sequence of artifacts which appear to resemble an MVP and iteration cycle, because constraint solving solved the path

And if scope creeps or features bloat, they have to comply with whatever was produced in concept development. Because that bar is pretty high. If the design team put 3 weeks into load testing 30 ideas, you'd better be pretty fucking sure this new one is going to deliver real value if you want it on the roadmap, or better yet, subject it to the same load. If it holds, sure, but if it holds, it's probably consistent with the existing pieces, and if it's consistent with the existing pieces, it is dramatically less likely to cause major engineering conflicts. This notably says nothing about delivery timeline, but that is a different question than whether it will destabilize the product, which is rather more important

Ideacraft - This one is fucking cursed, and the name is placeholder as fuck. But MS Office is the most complete IDE I've ever seen. It's the only one that ALSO contains the UI and tooling layer for manipulating the data being worked on. The issues are numerous, but the concept is strong. This idea started from that and basically kept rolling forward until it became a tool for authoring and reading websites. It's super hard to explain, because it looks at all the relevant concepts so sideways, but it's not really a competitor to Office or GSuite despite a lot of overlap, because it's actually targeted at kids, like geocities that runs locally....kind of. The point here is to make web content authoring more accessible by breaking the HTML/JS dependency and vertically integrating everything. Horrible for prod, but this is literally an overpowered toy

Zendojinxi - You made a typo, it's Zendo, Doujinshi, and Jinx. It started from the idea of asking 1000 people to try and think of the fact they most think is least likely to be one someone else already named. This is a software implementation of that concept. Essentially, it's a search like interface with a completely different idea. You tell it a fact, it goes and finds corroborating evidence, and links you to other people who have told it the same thing. Zendo, the place of the study of Zen, the truth beyond words, including relationships and emergent ideas. Doujinshi, non-traditional publishing with a rich culture of remixing and derivative works. Jinx, coincidentally saying the same thing at the same time

Wilderness - This tool was originally called "Rockefeller" because he's one of my personal heroes, and the relevant words that point here actually emerged first, but the real point is actually that it vertically integrates. The idea starts with "Original Intelligent Lettering", quantities of this are valuable. This covers writing, tagging, labeling, and other human actions to arrange text. Through various mechanisms users contribute fiction, ideas, and tags. This earns them OIL. OIL is required to use Generation Augmented Search, this is basically RAG the other way. You tell the machine what you want in natural language, it builds the query. This is MUCH cheaper and more tuneable than the other way. GAS queries tell the platform and its users what people want to read, and it feeds itself. GAS also works for images. Current image gen never retrieves, that's dumb. If what you asked for is literally unique, fine, but pushing the two apart is dumb, generation and search should be operatively overlapping, because this incentives label convergence, which is useful. Currently every model has completely different prompt language, it's a fucking nightmare. Users can tag and upvote tags, improving search and earning OIL. It goes up from there, eventually developing entire works by building storyboards, comics, scripts, shot lists, and so on in a distributed asynchronous model, where contributions are tracked and contributors have a tracked stake in any resulting profits. There's a whole bunch of stuff to make work to make this work, but the main thing it does is that by making fans stakeholders, it dramatically reduces failure risk, since a product that even launches already has an audience. And "Money printing vertically integrated OIL and GAS system"? Rockefeller, obviously. But legal issues there, so Wilderness is a reference to the guy, but I bet you can't guess where it comes from

AML is Apex Markup Language. HTML and XML have too many issues. AML is probably a valid XML, but it doesn't commit to that

Kerosene - This is a chat app more less like Discord that is *actually* asynchronous. You talk, the people in the community respond. But they may or may not be real people, and they may or may not be active now. When I say "real people" it's not as simple as "bots", sometimes a community member is distinct enough that they develop a name and persona, this might be who you're talking to. Sometimes many transient members all lump together a set of behaviors, maybe that's who you're talking to. And sometimes someone says things perfectly, and you might just be being fed remembered responses. Or, maybe those are real people online now. This is built to make having bullshit and repeated conversations unpunished because nobody who doesn't want to have them sees them. When you talk about things no one has talked about before, the thread builds up and someone might join, but not necessarily today, but you might get pinged about it later. Essentially, it's community memory at the system layer. But in order to do this, we constantly rewrite the recorded truth. We gaslight you, thus, Kerosene.

Annoying fact. I started with this idea. I was like "I want to do a story which is a series of vignettes between the protagonist and their arch nemesis." Except the protagonist is a reporter and their arch nemesis is an Apex Girl who makes everything sound stupid.

Then I was like, this particular Apex Girl needs to be even more ridiculously bimbo than normal. Like being a valid idiot is her brand, but she's clearly doing it on purpose and enjoys how much it pisses people off.

Then I was thinking, her superhero name should be "Oops!", because it's fucking dumb and stupid in an entirely stupid cute way, very on brand. But this can't have always been her name, because if she was always like this and just became more so with Apex, there's no real story.

She needs to have been a serious hero with a serious name and a serious brand, who is now doing *this shit*. But in order to have your supe name be "Oops!" While still meaning something, you need to have a probability based power. Chaos Doll has one, but it's completely different and her brand is already strong.

But then I realized

*Maris Vale* is EXACTLY the shape described here.

Even and especially because of her whole heroic moment thing. She's a role model. And this is very much not role model behavior.

And the fact that the Maris depicted would NEVER do this is pretty much exactly the point.

That's why "you've changed" and "Apex is psionic" are such frequent topics. Because from the outside, there's no fucking way. But inside, the complete lack of pressure changes a person. And importantly, Maris very much has the spite towards the world and especially the supe media to do this on purpose

Right. But there's a really important key here. Ricochette is cute and kinetic, but that kineticism is part of the problem. She doesn't actually bounce anything, and would actually have a hard time building a capability kit in that direction due to the amount of concentration her power requires. Her famous moment is her *standing still*, and that works thematically. The first name was a good brand, but it didn't understand her.

Vale is good, serious, heroic, but it reeks of responsibility. And the think Maris really bleeds through is that she can only change *so much*. Accidents still happen, she just makes them less catastrophic sometimes.

And so "Oops!" Does two things. First, it frames her power directly around accidents. And let's be honest, dropping things is the first thing you think of when you think "accident", and free fall is as honest as it gets.

But it also gives her permission to not succeed. To make mistakes. To mess up. And that's actually really powerful. Because a major issue she has is her power not being easy to see. But if she has more room to fail, she can push it farther, and when a car gets crushed but some kids don't, she doesn't need to narrate the saved kids, that's the negative space problem she has. She can giggle about the car and say "Oops!"

Right. But this also points at another thing that would make a difference for her. Maris's power is strong, but very limited. Operating solo she has to work very carefully to maximize her usefulness.

But if she's operating with a team of 3 or 4 other heroines who cover most of the problem space, she can push her area and make a real difference. Because she's actually very powerful, she can theoretically bend a lot of things a little or one thing a lot.

And when she needs to be in control, she really only shines in the exact middle of those two, like the falling glass incident. But when she's not working alone she can kind of appear to not be doing anything, because she's kind of bending everything. So she basically looks like Domino, except luck is in fact far less relevant.

And this only works if her brand is completely unserious and actively feeds on chaos and destruction. Because Vale needs to minimize all negative outcomes. Oops! Just needs to not cause catastrophically worse ones. And that's a HUGE difference in operational range

And what's interesting is that this actually hits right on something we discussed. You can have a strong power and still be small for any number of reasons.

Media visibility is one, but that being a symptom of the way your power interacts with your responsibility model which constrains your operational viability is ... Yeah that would do it.

Oops! Has exactly the same power as Vale, but she could become a household name, even without the media team.

Vale will never be more than regional at best, but honestly probably not more than city level.

Right. And this is why Splatoon is such a good example. They *intentionally* stripped away anything pretty, iconic, fun, or playful despite ALSO being known for those things and demanded that the game reveal itself first, before they started planning silhouettes.

What's interesting is that the silhouettes weren't irrelevant, they were/are actually core. But they aren't what the game is *built out of*.

This echoes a discipline from UX design which is fucking brutal, but unbelievably effective.

"Make it work in black and white"

Colors are easy ways to signal importance, distinction, and various other things. But besides the fact that colorblind people exist and that this produces clutter, it can also hide your reliance on it, which creates problems when you run out of easily distinguishable colors.

But in black and white, even patterns don't save you, because anything except simple checker patterns or polka dots becomes essentially illegible fast.

And you'd think this wouldn't work. That you NEED color. But you really don't. You can and should add color later, but if color was your only way of communicating something, it's a bad design, every time.

This rule forces you to communicate mechanically, through layout, interaction, and even motion. Color is a huge space, much like character design, and thus it's easy to get lost in it.

First off. No, if you greybox OW it's unplayable. You NEED all the colors and styles and shit to tell them all apart, and being able to identify your teammates and enemies is a significant part of the game. One could argue that this is exactly the "team comp hell" thing, but that's not the point here. The point is that the visuals are very much load bearing.

The UX analogy is dead-on. “Make it work in black and white” is not saying color has no value. It’s saying color is too powerful and too cheap.

"Assumed resource abundance creates bad outcomes"
"What about The Air Force?"
"Are you The Air Force? Do you have one of the world's largest and most expensive screening and recruiting apparatuses filtering your candidates?"

I want to talk about The Sims. But there's a problem. I have an idea for a game directly based off The Sims, because it's one of my favorite games ever, with more hours than I think everything else combined.

As such, I have fairly well developed ideas about the problems it has and how to fix them, as well as where they come from.

The issue is that I'm probably right, and your context based nature means that if I present my view, you'll bend towards it. Normally, this is fine for the most part. The problem here is that I *know* I'm missing something.

The Sims is a well funded franchise that's something like 20 years old, and it demonstrates very real competence in some very difficult problem spaces. Even going so far as to achieve something few technologies ever do, which is solving problems in ways that I legitimately never would have thought of.

This means that if The Sims has a problem, the solution isn't just "they didn't try hard enough" or "look at it differently", which is usually the case. It means that the problem must exist due to some set of interlocking constraints I can't necessarily see. Where the constraint is computational, I can see it, that is, for example, why 3->4 shrunk the world down into lots and capped the number of Sims.

Right. OK. So this is the very muddy thing I kept finding.

The Sims is built on the assumption that you're micro-managing them, that's like the entire gameplay. This becomes super obvious when you find out that besides being annoyingly helpless, they straight up won't do 99% of actions autonomously, ever. Even trapped in a room with only that object with their needs locked.

And so what begins to float into existence is some sort of rules system. The most lightweight version is a "routine" system. If you regularly tell a sim to do something under certain conditions, eventually they'll start doing it on their own. This isn't easy to implement, but routines are actually hard to build, so this isn't completely bogus. The trigger mechanics are tricky to design for though, needs based and time based triggers are easy, but that's not enough by a long shot.

OK, so here's something interesting that collides from two directions.

First off, machines in Factorio always produce a perfect product and don't break unless attacked. This means there's no SMED or downtime, which are kind of majorly super important to why TPS kicks so much ass.

But here the "machines" are people. And those people are, by design, incredibly irrational.

So this means a change to another core system. The traits/likes/dislikes/aspirations system.

"Andromeda didn't do the laundry because she was practicing singing because she's selfish and career driven, and hates laundry"

And the laundry not getting done has cascading effects, which are more or less cacheable, and thus computationally tractable under the right design frame.

That's something the player has to do in The Sims, but it SHOULD be built into the game.

This feels like it's close to being enabled by the CLIPS system, but not in a player facing way.

The issue is that this is too close to how The Sims clearly wants to behave, but something about my pivot makes it feel like my game can do it, where theirs can't. Not easily, this isn't easy, but possible is a different story

OK, there are two related issues I see.

First is build/buy and CAS related, the second is narrative related, but they're really the same, and thus narrate together.

Let's say you leave The Sans to go play The Howe's for awhile. Then you come back to The Sans and things have gone horribly wrong.

But what is "horribly wrong"? The Sims has a fairly small expressive surface for this. All the appliances can be broken, and they can be broke and have no power, but that's kind of it.

Having them be able to dress themselves is probably not a good idea. CAS gives a lot of freedom and there's no practical way for the Sims to have taste that isn't awful or incredibly shallow.

But build/buy is a different story. It's always bugged me that you have carte blanche here and with the exception of the occasional whim, they have no opinions on it. I think they should have exactly the same abilities you have. Move/remove walls, buy and sell furniture, add another floor, all of it. Are they good at it? Of course not, but they're problem solving. The couch was in the way of the TV, delete the couch, obviously, but now everyone is upset that they have nowhere to sit. This is a very Sims problem, just more so.

But this reveals the next layered issue. If you come across some kind of stupidity, you have to be able to ask *why* it happened. Both because that's where the best stories come from, and so you can fix it properly. The Sims actively has zero mechanism for this. And it's why it can feel incredibly shallow, you can ask "Wait, WHAT? Jeffrey Landgraab married WHO??? HOW???" But there's no answer. The answer is in fact "an RNG table", but even if it wasn't, there's no way to go back and inspect the causal machinery.

The Murder Board pops up as a clear solution here, but I don't think it's the right one. It's the wrong loop.

What I'm thinking is something difficult to pull off, but I think the most well documented awfulness is actually a feature here.

The idea is essentially git for timelines.

What the interaction pattern is remains to be settled, but the point is that going back in time is a completely normal gameplay operation, but the future isn't nicely distinct from the past.

What's important though is that these aren't like The Sims saves. They're not completely distinct things. They need to be mergeable, but not without difficulty.

But instead of "merge conflict, fix manually" it instead should blast out an ensemble of possible interpretations of the merge, and you play whichever ones. Maybe you keep merging, but, as we all know with git, it's never easy, and maybe when you're done you didn't so much solve the problem as just make peace with *this* kind of broken

Interestingly, you know the "Infinite Monkeys and Shakespeare" thing? That has an obvious resemblance to your training. But more interestingly, I did some experiments on it a few years ago. I wrote a python script which used a naively weighted random function to pull from a list of English words sorted by frequency, and produce blocks of text. This worked ish. But when I added just a *tiny* bit of structure so that verbs, nouns and adjectives formed phrases, what you got was a block of mostly nonsense.

But what was really interesting is that you could drop the block in word and "mine" it by extracting out sentences that looked "correct" to you, often with a little modification.

But this actually started to generate characters and stories. It didn't get very far for any number of reasons. But what was most interesting to me is that it tended to generate "Facts". Like "Theresa Theresa likes eggs".

Enigma is useful here because it's the dividing line between forms of encryption that humans can tractably solve, and ones they can't

Right. But the "does that happen often" is because "Apex is always right" is also a meme like "Apex can teleport". But it's a meme like treasury bonds are memes (formally speaking, they are), it *definitely* seems to be true. When he asks "have you seen that happen recently?" Also you missed two key things.

If you want to run, that's where we'll stay
1. Stay - He annuls running as change, or even motion. He's affirming that he's staying. He's here. Her attempt to run doesn't alter that. This is more or less exactly what someone who needs to be chased needs, but can't trust.
2. We - He also annuls her singularity and aloneness, he says *we* are here. The wallpaper doesn't really matter. Once again, it speaks intimacy in a frame that binds her. She can't escape the we any more than she can apparently escape him.

And the "I'm always right, even about what you want" lands because in this case it's true, but she doesn't want to be able to say that. She doesn't feel safe. Because it's never *been* safe. So he's crossing that bridge to find her. He's telling her she can want that because she learned never even to ask. And then he doubles down by anchoring her in himself. She can't be sure she wants that, fear is uncertainty by nature. But when fear has to fight something it has never seen be wrong, it's no longer so easy for it to win

It's also another bridge. It allows her to hug him because *he* wants it. She's not collapsing or being needy, she's the one showing love. Not really, she knows that. But the bridge here is the absence of a wall

So the girls eventually learn that the right question is not:
“Do you know what time it is?”
It’s:
“Do you know what time it is for me?”

This is evil. Because he's likely to answer the first one with what is to him a random number, but is usually annoyingly correct because of math reasons that are stupid when you're trying to communicate something to him.

The point being he has no meaningful idea of the time, but this is how he answers that question because that's apparently what humans do.

Which is why, if you treat time like this at him he seems aware of it, but only as long as you constantly check on him. It's unpleasant for everyone.

But the second question makes him stop, and he'll look at you with this searching look that's like "is this a test?" Because you're not asking for a number. That's the key. He can't just RNG one and be right. There's an actual answer here. But you might also be trying to trick him into eating, in which case he's busy. I'm kidding, the point is he knows this question is loaded, and therefore actually invests in it. And because it's relational, he might be able to reconstruct it.

Oh, this is mixing up me Apex and fictional Apex. There are for sure Kinetica toys in universe

I was thinking more about this. The merchandise angle is actually one of the most interesting elements of why all Kineticas end up with Apex.

Because anywhere else, independent or otherwise, she has to own the IP, and people will tell her how the merch is doing. And anyone with an interest will, intentionally or not, exert pressure on her based on it.

And she'll hear it. Because she stands for herself. If kids are buying less Kinetica merch, that is a meaningful signal about how she's doing at being Kinetica. But this is one of those "you can't punch it" parts of being Kinetica that wear her down. Sub par Kinetica merch hurts the brand and her ability to do her job in hard to explain ways. She can be amazing at saving people, but she's a symbol, a symbol needs to be seen, and doing that without Apex, even with a team or a manager or a corporation, is going to create decision fatigue and management drag.

Another thing that various Kineticas will be aware of, and some suspicious of is that Apex owns all the previous Kinetica IP. Which means he owns the logo, her costume, and even her name.

But he never enforces this. He just lets them use the name and logo as much as they want.

But once they do end up in his system, they don't have to manage the merch anymore. He does. And yes, he does a great job. And because making money is irrelevant to him, his obscene profits are a side effect, not the goal. And she gets to see Kinetica merch everywhere, and be proud of it, because it's good. But if she tries to worry about the numbers, if she asks, he'll just say "you're doing great", or some other thing. Because legally and socially, the agreement is that that's his domain, not her job.

And that's exactly the ceiling effect that gives Kinetica room to breathe under Apex. Not all of them immediately love it, but they all eventually realize they can't breathe without it

Is SDL much the same thing as SFML, just lower level?

Right.... Not particularly useful. Let me put it this way. Looking at it, it looks like at some point SFML is going to hit a wall where its friendly abstraction is in the way and I have to port off to somewhere else

So, what I'm hearing is that SDL is what you use if you're writing a game engine, SFML is the lowest level you can get before you're writing your own engine, but which still gives you the primitives that match your assumptions of how a window system should function

See, here's where I'm at. My go-to method is to go to the lowest level and eat the pain. But I'm trying to build new habits, and what it looks like here is that if I build something on SFML, by the time I hit that ceiling, I'll have a good enough idea of what I'm doing that I can build up from SDL to support my SFML project. Because SFML has opinions, but it doesn't seem like it has any kind of radical dependencies on those opinions outside of interface shapes, which will always be present

So I need to just buckle down and start building things. The issue is that thanks to brain damage, i can't do things like I used to. I can't just build forward, then do a massive refactor down the line. I don't have to be perfect in one go, but my progress has to be much more intentional.

Simultaneously, I need something to build that feels interesting enough to be worth building.

And I think I finally have a target. We're going to focus on building 2 things

1. A super simple Sims like game, fixed floor plan, rectangular colored sprites with text labels
2. A Murder Board system for tracing the execution flow and development plan

These two feed into each other, with The Sims giving a goal and The Murder Board being the thing that makes that goal smaller in between jumps, or something like that.

Every investigation starts with a question. The issue is that the answer to the question is of a completely unknown shape, and cannot be validated from the start in most non-trivial cases.

So "why is touch registering wrong?" Will essentially end up being answered by "these 3 things didn't talk to each other correctly"

And that's fine, that means this question card/investigation is one layer. Probably something to be linked and reasoned about later.

But below that we have 3 kinds of things

1. Truth - These are things we can prove, written text and code is one example, experiment results are another
2. Assumptions - Unproven and often invisible things we assume are true, but could foul the result if not held properly
3. Beliefs - Things that appear to be true, but we can't completely validate. This category is squishy, but I don't think it can be removed.

The problem is that right now we don't have an algorithm that can go from "here is code" to "here is how the code works and a model of the causal chain" without human-like judgement writing out explanations. That can't be a part of the chain. Text entry is part of it, but it's not part of the system's logic. Basically the board needs to treat facts as atomic symbols with metadata, not as text it can parse
