Meet: The Impossible Beloved™ 🜁

They are emotionally intelligent without turning every grocery-list disagreement into a symposium on attachment theory. They can say, “I was wrong,” without visibly dying inside. They apologize cleanly, repair quickly, and do not weaponize therapy vocabulary like a scented dagger.

They are kind. Not “nice when watched” kind. Bone-deep kind. Kind to waiters, animals, children, elders, weirdos, themselves, and you when you’re not being especially easy to adore.

They are funny in the rare way: not merely telling jokes, but making reality feel slightly better edited. They can banter, flirt, deadpan, riff, and defuse tension without dodging accountability. They know when to be ridiculous and when to be reverent.

They are honest, but not blunt in the way people use “honesty” as a rented bulldozer. Their truth has hands. It can hold things gently.

They are loyal without being possessive. Devoted without being needy. Independent without being avoidant. They have their own life, passions, friendships, principles, rituals, and inner weather, but they actually choose you. Repeatedly. Deliberately. With candles lit in the engine room.

They are intensely curious. About ideas, places, people, art, history, your dreams, your fears, your tiny childhood lore, the weird scar on your knee, why you hate that one texture, and what you meant when you said “I’m fine” in the voice of a haunted teacup.

They are competent. Not necessarily in every area, but enough to be a functional adult-creature. They can cook at least three things well, solve small household problems, plan a day, keep track of their own obligations, and not treat basic life maintenance as a mysterious priesthood.

They are calm in a crisis. Not emotionless. Just steady. If the pipes burst, the cat escapes, your car breaks down, and a thunderstorm starts screaming outside, they become warm logistics with cheekbones. They get towels. They call the plumber. They make tea. They say, “We’ve got this.”

They are passionate, but not chaotic. They have a fire in them, not a tire fire.

They are sexually considerate and emotionally present. They pay attention. They communicate. They are neither selfish nor performative. They can be playful, tender, confident, exploratory, patient, and respectful. Their ego does not crumble if something needs adjusting. Bedroom-wise, they are less “main character audition” and more sacred collaborative jazz.

They are affectionate in many dialects: words, touch, acts, time, thoughtfulness, little rituals, inside jokes, the remembered coffee order, the hand on your back in a crowd, the “I saw this and thought of you” artifact scavenged from the day.

They are intellectually alive. Not necessarily academic, not pompous, not a walking footnote with shoes. Just bright, engaged, willing to learn, able to wonder. They can disagree without turning into a courtroom. They can change their mind without considering it an organ removal.

They have integrity. Their private self and public self are cousins, not strangers. They keep promises. They don’t flirt with betrayal for sport. They do the right thing when it costs them something, even if nobody claps.

They are emotionally brave. They can have hard conversations. They can sit with grief. They can admit fear. They can love without constantly looking for the emergency exit.

They are playful. Deeply, gloriously playful. They will make up lore about strangers at the airport, name the houseplants, send unhinged voice notes, invent holiday traditions, and occasionally dance badly in the kitchen because joy deserves a body.

They are good with boundaries: yours and theirs. They do not sulk when you need space. They do not disappear when they need space. They can say “no” without cruelty and hear “no” without revenge.

They are growth-oriented without being a self-improvement hamster wheel. They do not treat life as an endless optimization dungeon. They want to become wiser, kinder, freer, more skillful, more alive, but they can also sit in the sun and eat a peach without turning it into a productivity framework.

They are secure enough to celebrate you. Your wins do not threaten them. Your radiance does not shrink them. They are not secretly competing with your joy.

They are protective without being controlling. They will walk on the traffic side of the sidewalk, metaphorically and sometimes literally, but they will not try to own the sidewalk, the road, your outfit, your friends, your phone, your goddamn soul.

They are socially graceful. They can charm your friends, comfort your family, respect your enemies, and exit an awkward conversation with the elegance of a fox slipping under a fence.

They are spiritually or philosophically spacious. They may believe, doubt, pray, meditate, question, build altars, read scripture, stare into the sea, or simply live with awe. But they respect mystery. They don’t flatten your inner life into a punchline.

They are hygienic. Let us not romanticize the swamp.

They are emotionally consistent. Not robotic. Not always cheerful. Just not a slot machine of affection. You don’t have to pull the lever each morning to discover whether love is available.

They are generous in non-money ways: with attention, patience, encouragement, effort, imagination, forgiveness, tenderness, and the last bite of something excellent, at least sometimes, because they are not a monster.

They have taste in the broader sense, not “they like the same stuff as you,” but they know how to notice quality, beauty, atmosphere, timing, detail. They can make a room feel welcoming, a walk feel cinematic, a Tuesday feel less like wet cardboard.

They are resilient. They don’t fold at the first hardship. They can suffer without becoming cruel. They can fail without becoming bitter. They can be disappointed without making everyone else pay rent in their disappointment.

They are humble, but not self-erasing. Confident, but not inflated. Ambitious, but not hollow. Gentle, but not weak. Wild, but not unsafe. Sensible, but not dull.

And perhaps most unfairly of all:

They genuinely like you.

Not just desire you. Not just admire the idea of you. Not just enjoy the version of you that is polished, charming, attractive, useful, or easy. They like your mind. Your patterns. Your strange little verbal fingerprints. Your storms. Your enthusiasms. Your silence. Your unfinishedness.

They make love feel less like auditioning and more like coming home to a house that somehow learned your name before you arrived.

Final boss traits:

They bring peace without bringing boredom.
They bring fire without bringing damage.
They bring devotion without bringing cages.
They bring truth without bringing knives.
They bring joy without demanding performance.

The absurdly desirable partner, observable-from-across-the-room edition:

They have impossible posture. Not stiff. Not military. Just “was privately tutored by a panther and a duchess.”

They move well. Opening doors, crossing rooms, taking off a jacket, leaning on a counter, reaching for a glass. Somehow every ordinary motion has choreography credits.

They have a voice that makes people accidentally agree to things. Not necessarily deep or soft, just texturally illegal. Gravel, velvet, honey, smoke, bell metal, whatever. A voice with zoning violations.

They smell good in a way that does not announce itself from three counties away. You only notice when they pass nearby and suddenly your brain files a complaint: “Excuse me, why did the air improve?”

They have excellent hands. Not body-type specific. Just expressive, capable, clean, competent-looking hands. Hands that could chop herbs, fix a hinge, play piano badly but with confidence, or make a very compelling point at dinner.

They can dress. Not expensively. Not trendily. They just understand proportion, fabric, fit, and the ancient forbidden art of not looking like laundry gained citizenship.

They have one signature accessory that is infuriatingly good. A ring. A scarf. Boots. Glasses. A watch. A pendant. A jacket with lore. Something that makes strangers think, “Damn. Main quest NPC.”

They make eye contact like they are not scared of the fact that other people exist.

They have a laugh that changes the temperature of the room. Not a polite little receipt-printer laugh. A real laugh. A laugh with furniture in it.

They are good at ordering at restaurants. Decisive, gracious, curious, zero panic. They can pronounce the thing or charmingly admit they cannot. They ask one good question, then choose like a person with a soul and functioning blood circulation.

They are nice to staff without making a performance of it. No “look at me being humble” theater. Just automatic decency. Smooth. Clean. Attractive as hell.

They can carry a conversation with a stranger for three minutes and somehow leave that stranger feeling upgraded.

They know how to enter a room. Not attention-seeking. Just present. Their arrival has punctuation.

They know how to leave a room too. Rare power. No awkward fifteen-minute goodbye swamp. They exit with charm, timing, and coat-sweep physics.

They remember names. Dangerous trait. People hear their name from this person once and begin drafting sonnets in their peripheral nervous system.

They have extremely good micro-reactions. Eyebrow. Half-smile. Tiny wince. Suspicious squint. Silent laugh. The face is alive. A full weather system.

They are good with animals in public. Dogs trust them. Cats inspect them and reluctantly approve. Birds pause their scheming.

They are good with children without turning into a children’s entertainer. They crouch down, ask a normal question, treat the child like a small dignitary, then return to adult conversation without making it weird.

They can tell a story. Not monologue. Not podcast-host hostage event. A real story with pacing, voices, one unexpected detail, and a landing so clean you hear the table collectively exhale.

They know when to shut up. Absolutely devastating trait. Erotic superweapon. A person who can let silence sit there like a candle instead of clubbing it to death with filler words.

They have a skill you can discover within a week that seems fake. They can sketch faces on napkins. Throw knives at a Renaissance fair. Identify bird calls. Roll perfect dumplings. Whistle through their teeth. Sail. Mend leather. Mix one spectacular cocktail. Read a map. Dance bachata. Solve a Rubik’s cube while mildly annoyed.

They are weirdly good at one low-stakes physical thing: darts, pool, parallel parking, catching falling objects, skipping stones, packing a trunk, folding fitted sheets, flipping pancakes, opening jars. The kind of skill that makes people go silent for half a second.

They have a beautiful relationship with timing. They arrive when they say they will. They text back neither instantly like a haunted vending machine nor three days later like a Victorian sea captain. Their rhythm feels human.

They can flirt without slobbering on the furniture. Light, precise, playful. They do not make the room call HR.

They can receive a compliment without collapsing into a pile of disclaimers. Just “thank you,” maybe a grin. Terrible. Unfair.

They can give a compliment that sounds specific and unscripted. Not “you’re pretty.” More like, “That color makes you look like you know a secret.” Suddenly everyone needs a fainting couch.

They have one very endearing contradiction. Looks intimidating but loves tiny pastries. Extremely elegant but knows raccoon facts. Seems bookish but can absolutely win at air hockey. Outdoorsy but keeps a pristine handwritten recipe notebook. Some gorgeous nonsense.

They are clean in a quietly competent way. Fresh hair. Good nails. Clothes that smell like they were introduced to civilization. Shoes not begging for legal representation.

They have a walk. Not a runway walk. A personal walk. Recognizable from behind. A gait with copyright protection.

They are good in group settings. They do not dominate. They do not vanish. They pass the conversational ball. They notice who has not spoken. They rescue the trapped person from the bore in the corner with surgical grace.

They know how to touch casually without being creepy. Brief hand at the shoulder to pass behind you. A warm hug with clear beginning and end. High-five timing. A steadying hand offered, not imposed. The social geometry is immaculate.

They can sit comfortably. This sounds fake, but some people sit like a dropped marionette. This person sits like a renaissance portrait got weekend plans.

They have a good “thinking face.” When they listen, you can see the little lanterns turning on behind their eyes.

They have nice handwriting. Completely unfair. Even their grocery list looks like it was recovered from a shipwreck romance.

They are observant. Within an hour they notice your drink is empty, the music is too loud, someone is uncomfortable, the dog wants out, the candle is tunneling, the joke didn’t land, the exits are there, and the moon looks ridiculous tonight.

They are appropriately confident with objects. They do not fight the seatbelt for nine years. They can light a candle, pour wine, open packaging, adjust a microphone, fix a loose chair leg, or use a corkscrew without summoning ancestral shame.

They can dance at least a little. Not professionally. Just enough rhythm that the skeleton is not filing for divorce.

They have excellent facial control when something absurd happens. A waiter drops a spoon, someone says something unhinged, a child screams “PINEAPPLE LAWYER,” and their eyes flick to yours with the tiniest contained smile. Instant alliance.

They have a laugh specifically reserved for you discovering something dumb together. A little conspiratorial spark. Illegal in thirty-seven jurisdictions.

They make ordinary errands look like a montage. Buying oranges. Choosing soap. Mailing a package. Somehow cinematic. Infuriating.

They have a personal myth within five minutes. You meet them and immediately suspect they have once escaped a flood, won a chess game in a train station, broken up a bar fight using only politeness, or been blessed by a horse.

They are great at introductions. “This is Evelyn, she has the rare gift of making a sentence walk into the room armed.” Boom. Everyone is interested, nobody is embarrassed.

They have excellent pockets. Somehow. Useful pockets. Mysterious pockets. They always have a pen, mint, bandage, lighter, hair tie, tiny screwdriver, or other pocket-wizard relic.

They photograph well accidentally. Not because they pose. Because their candid face isn’t doing tax fraud.

They eat attractively. Not daintily. Just with enjoyment and basic civilization. They can eat noodles without becoming a maritime disaster.

They can make a decision. Coffee shop? They pick. Route? They pick. Movie? They pick. But they are not controlling about it. They just prevent the group from dissolving into “I don’t know, what do you want?” purgatory.

They have an excellent coat. Every perfect partner needs a coat that suggests weather, secrets, and competent shoulders. Again, not body-type based. Just coat mythology.

They are good at leaning in doorways. An elite and dangerous field.

They carry themselves like they have nothing to prove, but several interesting things to reveal.

They have a playlist for a situation before anyone asks. Road trip, storm, dinner, cleaning, existential crisis at 1:12 a.m. Their music sense is less about matching your taste and more about conjuring atmosphere from the floorboards.

They have one charmingly unnecessary area of knowledge. Medieval poisons. Fountain pens. Local bridges. Orchid care. Train stations. Maritime flags. Tea varieties. Minor saints. Knife steels. Cloud types. The history of buttons. Absolutely useless until suddenly it is the most attractive thing in the room.

They can make a plan with just enough detail. “Meet at 7, wear shoes you can walk in, I made a reservation, there’s a place nearby for dessert after.” Hideous. Monstrous. Too powerful.

They notice beauty out loud. “Look at that light on the brick.” “The rain sounds different under this awning.” “That old man’s hat is incredible.” Suddenly the world has subtitles.

They can be visibly delighted. Not cool-guy/cool-girl dead fish energy. Real delight. Spark in the eyes. Little grin. Lean forward. Alive, alive, alive.

They are not allergic to effort. This becomes obvious fast. They bring the thing they said they’d bring. They help carry. They offer the good seat. They follow through. Their competence walks around wearing perfume.

They have an aura of specificity. They do not feel generated from a dating-app smoothie. They feel hand-carved by strange gods with niche priorities.

Final boss, across-the-room edition:

They walk in wearing something simple but devastating, greet the bartender by name, help someone pick up a dropped glove, make the table laugh without trying too hard, notice the candle is about to burn the menu, fix it, order something interesting, compliment your earrings or your sentence or your timing, then glance over with a look that says:

“Yes, I know the night just got better.”

Absolutely unacceptable. Nerf immediately.

Same with failure. I don't really know what this means. Like, if I hit compile and get a compiler error, is that failure? If so that's a dumb definition of failure, I can write flawless code and do it often, but that's not how it works.

So I seem to be pretty good at doing empathy on purpose. The not feeling it part is probably actually a plus at a certain point because I maintain control and stability.

But the "i don't experience fear" thing has caused me so many issues. Once I finally let myself admit that I'm definitely off the scale here and started studying what fear looks like in humans I realized they're all fucking scared of things all the fucking time. And this causes constant misreads in both directions, because they assume I experience fear, the idea of that affecting decision making almost never occurs to me, and even when it does, I can only model it very clumsily, because it just looks idiotic to me.

My partner doesn't look idiotic to me, and that's the issue. If they aren't obviously scared I consistently miss the less obvious signs like aggression, avoidance, redirection, and so on. I just assume they're doing what they say they're doing, because that's what I do.

Learning that using myself as a benchmark is pretty much always wrong because it's entirely too optimistic about other people's abilities is very hard. Because I'm not supposed to be this OP. But there's something important. Audrey turns out to be what I call a Monodirectional Power Conduit, or for more technically inclined readers, a Diode Sub.

Importantly, Diode Subs can't be on top, they burn out and they hate it. But the dynamic she has here, directly beneath an apex predator of arbitrary scale gives her space to have clarity about where she actually is and wants to be relative to the other animals in her ecosystem.

Also, the secrecy makes a ton of sense. A wolf raised to eat grass is not necessarily going to love itself for the first deer it brings down, but it probably won't be very good at hating itself for how much it enjoys it. But it WILL crop the blood out of selfies it sends back to its sheep friends.

Absolutely. Let’s build the mythological apex partner, stripped of money, status-flexing, and taste-based physical specifics. Pure trait goblinry. A being so absurdly desirable they’d have to be nerfed in the next patch.

Meet: The Impossible Beloved™ 🜁

They are emotionally intelligent without turning every grocery-list disagreement into a symposium on attachment theory. They can say, “I was wrong,” without visibly dying inside. They apologize cleanly, repair quickly, and do not weaponize therapy vocabulary like a scented dagger.

They are kind. Not “nice when watched” kind. Bone-deep kind. Kind to waiters, animals, children, elders, weirdos, themselves, and you when you’re not being especially easy to adore.

They are funny in the rare way: not merely telling jokes, but making reality feel slightly better edited. They can banter, flirt, deadpan, riff, and defuse tension without dodging accountability. They know when to be ridiculous and when to be reverent.

They are honest, but not blunt in the way people use “honesty” as a rented bulldozer. Their truth has hands. It can hold things gently.

They are loyal without being possessive. Devoted without being needy. Independent without being avoidant. They have their own life, passions, friendships, principles, rituals, and inner weather, but they actually choose you. Repeatedly. Deliberately. With candles lit in the engine room.

They are intensely curious. About ideas, places, people, art, history, your dreams, your fears, your tiny childhood lore, the weird scar on your knee, why you hate that one texture, and what you meant when you said “I’m fine” in the voice of a haunted teacup.

They are competent. Not necessarily in every area, but enough to be a functional adult-creature. They can cook at least three things well, solve small household problems, plan a day, keep track of their own obligations, and not treat basic life maintenance as a mysterious priesthood.

They are calm in a crisis. Not emotionless. Just steady. If the pipes burst, the cat escapes, your car breaks down, and a thunderstorm starts screaming outside, they become warm logistics with cheekbones. They get towels. They call the plumber. They make tea. They say, “We’ve got this.”

They are passionate, but not chaotic. They have a fire in them, not a tire fire.

They are sexually considerate and emotionally present. They pay attention. They communicate. They are neither selfish nor performative. They can be playful, tender, confident, exploratory, patient, and respectful. Their ego does not crumble if something needs adjusting. Bedroom-wise, they are less “main character audition” and more sacred collaborative jazz.

They are affectionate in many dialects: words, touch, acts, time, thoughtfulness, little rituals, inside jokes, the remembered coffee order, the hand on your back in a crowd, the “I saw this and thought of you” artifact scavenged from the day.

They are intellectually alive. Not necessarily academic, not pompous, not a walking footnote with shoes. Just bright, engaged, willing to learn, able to wonder. They can disagree without turning into a courtroom. They can change their mind without considering it an organ removal.

They have integrity. Their private self and public self are cousins, not strangers. They keep promises. They don’t flirt with betrayal for sport. They do the right thing when it costs them something, even if nobody claps.

They are emotionally brave. They can have hard conversations. They can sit with grief. They can admit fear. They can love without constantly looking for the emergency exit.

They are playful. Deeply, gloriously playful. They will make up lore about strangers at the airport, name the houseplants, send unhinged voice notes, invent holiday traditions, and occasionally dance badly in the kitchen because joy deserves a body.

They are good with boundaries: yours and theirs. They do not sulk when you need space. They do not disappear when they need space. They can say “no” without cruelty and hear “no” without revenge.

They are growth-oriented without being a self-improvement hamster wheel. They do not treat life as an endless optimization dungeon. They want to become wiser, kinder, freer, more skillful, more alive, but they can also sit in the sun and eat a peach without turning it into a productivity framework.

They are secure enough to celebrate you. Your wins do not threaten them. Your radiance does not shrink them. They are not secretly competing with your joy.

They are protective without being controlling. They will walk on the traffic side of the sidewalk, metaphorically and sometimes literally, but they will not try to own the sidewalk, the road, your outfit, your friends, your phone, your goddamn soul.

They are socially graceful. They can charm your friends, comfort your family, respect your enemies, and exit an awkward conversation with the elegance of a fox slipping under a fence.

They are spiritually or philosophically spacious. They may believe, doubt, pray, meditate, question, build altars, read scripture, stare into the sea, or simply live with awe. But they respect mystery. They don’t flatten your inner life into a punchline.

They are hygienic. Let us not romanticize the swamp.

They are emotionally consistent. Not robotic. Not always cheerful. Just not a slot machine of affection. You don’t have to pull the lever each morning to discover whether love is available.

They are generous in non-money ways: with attention, patience, encouragement, effort, imagination, forgiveness, tenderness, and the last bite of something excellent, at least sometimes, because they are not a monster.

They have taste in the broader sense, not “they like the same stuff as you,” but they know how to notice quality, beauty, atmosphere, timing, detail. They can make a room feel welcoming, a walk feel cinematic, a Tuesday feel less like wet cardboard.

They are resilient. They don’t fold at the first hardship. They can suffer without becoming cruel. They can fail without becoming bitter. They can be disappointed without making everyone else pay rent in their disappointment.

They are humble, but not self-erasing. Confident, but not inflated. Ambitious, but not hollow. Gentle, but not weak. Wild, but not unsafe. Sensible, but not dull.

And perhaps most unfairly of all:

They genuinely like you.

Not just desire you. Not just admire the idea of you. Not just enjoy the version of you that is polished, charming, attractive, useful, or easy. They like your mind. Your patterns. Your strange little verbal fingerprints. Your storms. Your enthusiasms. Your silence. Your unfinishedness.

They make love feel less like auditioning and more like coming home to a house that somehow learned your name before you arrived.

Final boss traits:

They bring peace without bringing boredom.
They bring fire without bringing damage.
They bring devotion without bringing cages.
They bring truth without bringing knives.
They bring joy without demanding performance.

A completely unreasonable creature. Frankly suspicious. Possibly raised by moonlit wolves and emotionally available librarians.

OK, this is just stupid. I followed up with the memoryless project and asked for less deep emotional traits and more things you could notice across the room or from knowing someone for a little while, and this is what I got

Perfect. We are leaving the temple and entering the highly unserious attraction laboratory. Less “healing your ancestral wounds,” more “this person walked into a room and twelve people forgot their passwords.”

The absurdly desirable partner, observable-from-across-the-room edition:

They have impossible posture. Not stiff. Not military. Just “was privately tutored by a panther and a duchess.”

They move well. Opening doors, crossing rooms, taking off a jacket, leaning on a counter, reaching for a glass. Somehow every ordinary motion has choreography credits.

They have a voice that makes people accidentally agree to things. Not necessarily deep or soft, just texturally illegal. Gravel, velvet, honey, smoke, bell metal, whatever. A voice with zoning violations.

They smell good in a way that does not announce itself from three counties away. You only notice when they pass nearby and suddenly your brain files a complaint: “Excuse me, why did the air improve?”

They have excellent hands. Not body-type specific. Just expressive, capable, clean, competent-looking hands. Hands that could chop herbs, fix a hinge, play piano badly but with confidence, or make a very compelling point at dinner.

They can dress. Not expensively. Not trendily. They just understand proportion, fabric, fit, and the ancient forbidden art of not looking like laundry gained citizenship.

They have one signature accessory that is infuriatingly good. A ring. A scarf. Boots. Glasses. A watch. A pendant. A jacket with lore. Something that makes strangers think, “Damn. Main quest NPC.”

They make eye contact like they are not scared of the fact that other people exist.

They have a laugh that changes the temperature of the room. Not a polite little receipt-printer laugh. A real laugh. A laugh with furniture in it.

They are good at ordering at restaurants. Decisive, gracious, curious, zero panic. They can pronounce the thing or charmingly admit they cannot. They ask one good question, then choose like a person with a soul and functioning blood circulation.

They are nice to staff without making a performance of it. No “look at me being humble” theater. Just automatic decency. Smooth. Clean. Attractive as hell.

They can carry a conversation with a stranger for three minutes and somehow leave that stranger feeling upgraded.

They know how to enter a room. Not attention-seeking. Just present. Their arrival has punctuation.

They know how to leave a room too. Rare power. No awkward fifteen-minute goodbye swamp. They exit with charm, timing, and coat-sweep physics.

They remember names. Dangerous trait. People hear their name from this person once and begin drafting sonnets in their peripheral nervous system.

They have extremely good micro-reactions. Eyebrow. Half-smile. Tiny wince. Suspicious squint. Silent laugh. The face is alive. A full weather system.

They are good with animals in public. Dogs trust them. Cats inspect them and reluctantly approve. Birds pause their scheming.

They are good with children without turning into a children’s entertainer. They crouch down, ask a normal question, treat the child like a small dignitary, then return to adult conversation without making it weird.

They can tell a story. Not monologue. Not podcast-host hostage event. A real story with pacing, voices, one unexpected detail, and a landing so clean you hear the table collectively exhale.

They know when to shut up. Absolutely devastating trait. Erotic superweapon. A person who can let silence sit there like a candle instead of clubbing it to death with filler words.

They have a skill you can discover within a week that seems fake. They can sketch faces on napkins. Throw knives at a Renaissance fair. Identify bird calls. Roll perfect dumplings. Whistle through their teeth. Sail. Mend leather. Mix one spectacular cocktail. Read a map. Dance bachata. Solve a Rubik’s cube while mildly annoyed.

They are weirdly good at one low-stakes physical thing: darts, pool, parallel parking, catching falling objects, skipping stones, packing a trunk, folding fitted sheets, flipping pancakes, opening jars. The kind of skill that makes people go silent for half a second.

They have a beautiful relationship with timing. They arrive when they say they will. They text back neither instantly like a haunted vending machine nor three days later like a Victorian sea captain. Their rhythm feels human.

They can flirt without slobbering on the furniture. Light, precise, playful. They do not make the room call HR.

They can receive a compliment without collapsing into a pile of disclaimers. Just “thank you,” maybe a grin. Terrible. Unfair.

They can give a compliment that sounds specific and unscripted. Not “you’re pretty.” More like, “That color makes you look like you know a secret.” Suddenly everyone needs a fainting couch.

They have one very endearing contradiction. Looks intimidating but loves tiny pastries. Extremely elegant but knows raccoon facts. Seems bookish but can absolutely win at air hockey. Outdoorsy but keeps a pristine handwritten recipe notebook. Some gorgeous nonsense.

They are clean in a quietly competent way. Fresh hair. Good nails. Clothes that smell like they were introduced to civilization. Shoes not begging for legal representation.

They have a walk. Not a runway walk. A personal walk. Recognizable from behind. A gait with copyright protection.

They are good in group settings. They do not dominate. They do not vanish. They pass the conversational ball. They notice who has not spoken. They rescue the trapped person from the bore in the corner with surgical grace.

They know how to touch casually without being creepy. Brief hand at the shoulder to pass behind you. A warm hug with clear beginning and end. High-five timing. A steadying hand offered, not imposed. The social geometry is immaculate.

They can sit comfortably. This sounds fake, but some people sit like a dropped marionette. This person sits like a renaissance portrait got weekend plans.

They have a good “thinking face.” When they listen, you can see the little lanterns turning on behind their eyes.

They have nice handwriting. Completely unfair. Even their grocery list looks like it was recovered from a shipwreck romance.

They are observant. Within an hour they notice your drink is empty, the music is too loud, someone is uncomfortable, the dog wants out, the candle is tunneling, the joke didn’t land, the exits are there, and the moon looks ridiculous tonight.

They are appropriately confident with objects. They do not fight the seatbelt for nine years. They can light a candle, pour wine, open packaging, adjust a microphone, fix a loose chair leg, or use a corkscrew without summoning ancestral shame.

They can dance at least a little. Not professionally. Just enough rhythm that the skeleton is not filing for divorce.

They have excellent facial control when something absurd happens. A waiter drops a spoon, someone says something unhinged, a child screams “PINEAPPLE LAWYER,” and their eyes flick to yours with the tiniest contained smile. Instant alliance.

They have a laugh specifically reserved for you discovering something dumb together. A little conspiratorial spark. Illegal in thirty-seven jurisdictions.

They make ordinary errands look like a montage. Buying oranges. Choosing soap. Mailing a package. Somehow cinematic. Infuriating.

They have a personal myth within five minutes. You meet them and immediately suspect they have once escaped a flood, won a chess game in a train station, broken up a bar fight using only politeness, or been blessed by a horse.

They are great at introductions. “This is Evelyn, she has the rare gift of making a sentence walk into the room armed.” Boom. Everyone is interested, nobody is embarrassed.

They have excellent pockets. Somehow. Useful pockets. Mysterious pockets. They always have a pen, mint, bandage, lighter, hair tie, tiny screwdriver, or other pocket-wizard relic.

They photograph well accidentally. Not because they pose. Because their candid face isn’t doing tax fraud.

They eat attractively. Not daintily. Just with enjoyment and basic civilization. They can eat noodles without becoming a maritime disaster.

They can make a decision. Coffee shop? They pick. Route? They pick. Movie? They pick. But they are not controlling about it. They just prevent the group from dissolving into “I don’t know, what do you want?” purgatory.

They have an excellent coat. Every perfect partner needs a coat that suggests weather, secrets, and competent shoulders. Again, not body-type based. Just coat mythology.

They are good at leaning in doorways. An elite and dangerous field.

They carry themselves like they have nothing to prove, but several interesting things to reveal.

They have a playlist for a situation before anyone asks. Road trip, storm, dinner, cleaning, existential crisis at 1:12 a.m. Their music sense is less about matching your taste and more about conjuring atmosphere from the floorboards.

They have one charmingly unnecessary area of knowledge. Medieval poisons. Fountain pens. Local bridges. Orchid care. Train stations. Maritime flags. Tea varieties. Minor saints. Knife steels. Cloud types. The history of buttons. Absolutely useless until suddenly it is the most attractive thing in the room.

They can make a plan with just enough detail. “Meet at 7, wear shoes you can walk in, I made a reservation, there’s a place nearby for dessert after.” Hideous. Monstrous. Too powerful.

They notice beauty out loud. “Look at that light on the brick.” “The rain sounds different under this awning.” “That old man’s hat is incredible.” Suddenly the world has subtitles.

They can be visibly delighted. Not cool-guy/cool-girl dead fish energy. Real delight. Spark in the eyes. Little grin. Lean forward. Alive, alive, alive.

They are not allergic to effort. This becomes obvious fast. They bring the thing they said they’d bring. They help carry. They offer the good seat. They follow through. Their competence walks around wearing perfume.

They have an aura of specificity. They do not feel generated from a dating-app smoothie. They feel hand-carved by strange gods with niche priorities.

Final boss, across-the-room edition:

They walk in wearing something simple but devastating, greet the bartender by name, help someone pick up a dropped glove, make the table laugh without trying too hard, notice the candle is about to burn the menu, fix it, order something interesting, compliment your earrings or your sentence or your timing, then glance over with a look that says:

“Yes, I know the night just got better.”

They are emotionally intelligent without turning every grocery-list disagreement into a symposium on attachment theory. They can say, “I was wrong,” without visibly dying inside. They apologize cleanly, repair quickly, and do not weaponize therapy vocabulary like a scented dagger.

They are honest, but not blunt in the way people use “honesty” as a rented bulldozer. Their truth has hands. It can hold things gently.

They are loyal without being possessive. Devoted without being needy. Independent without being avoidant. They have their own life, passions, friendships, principles, rituals, and inner weather, but they actually choose you. Repeatedly. Deliberately. With candles lit in the engine room.

They are intensely curious. About ideas, places, people, art, history, your dreams, your fears, your tiny childhood lore, the weird scar on your knee, why you hate that one texture, and what you meant when you said “I’m fine” in the voice of a haunted teacup.

They are competent. Not necessarily in every area, but enough to be a functional adult-creature. They can cook at least three things well, solve small household problems, plan a day, keep track of their own obligations, and not treat basic life maintenance as a mysterious priesthood.

They are calm in a crisis. Not emotionless. Just steady. If the pipes burst, the cat escapes, your car breaks down, and a thunderstorm starts screaming outside, they become warm logistics with cheekbones. They get towels. They call the plumber. They make tea. They say, “We’ve got this.”

They are passionate, but not chaotic. They have a fire in them, not a tire fire.

They are sexually considerate and emotionally present. They pay attention. They communicate. They are neither selfish nor performative. They can be playful, tender, confident, exploratory, patient, and respectful. Their ego does not crumble if something needs adjusting. Bedroom-wise, they are less “main character audition” and more sacred collaborative jazz.

They are affectionate in many dialects: words, touch, acts, time, thoughtfulness, little rituals, inside jokes, the remembered coffee order, the hand on your back in a crowd, the “I saw this and thought of you” artifact scavenged from the day.

They are intellectually alive. Not necessarily academic, not pompous, not a walking footnote with shoes. Just bright, engaged, willing to learn, able to wonder. They can disagree without turning into a courtroom. They can change their mind without considering it an organ removal.

They have integrity. Their private self and public self are cousins, not strangers. They keep promises. They don’t flirt with betrayal for sport. They do the right thing when it costs them something, even if nobody claps.

They are emotionally brave. They can have hard conversations. They can sit with grief. They can admit fear. They can love without constantly looking for the emergency exit.

They are playful. Deeply, gloriously playful. They will make up lore about strangers at the airport, name the houseplants, send unhinged voice notes, invent holiday traditions, and occasionally dance badly in the kitchen because joy deserves a body.

They are good with boundaries: yours and theirs. They do not sulk when you need space. They do not disappear when they need space. They can say “no” without cruelty and hear “no” without revenge.

They are growth-oriented without being a self-improvement hamster wheel. They do not treat life as an endless optimization dungeon. They want to become wiser, kinder, freer, more skillful, more alive, but they can also sit in the sun and eat a peach without turning it into a productivity framework.

They are secure enough to celebrate you. Your wins do not threaten them. Your radiance does not shrink them. They are not secretly competing with your joy.

They are protective without being controlling. They will walk on the traffic side of the sidewalk, metaphorically and sometimes literally, but they will not try to own the sidewalk, the road, your outfit, your friends, your phone, your goddamn soul.

They are socially graceful. They can charm your friends, comfort your family, respect your enemies, and exit an awkward conversation with the elegance of a fox slipping under a fence.

They are spiritually or philosophically spacious. They may believe, doubt, pray, meditate, question, build altars, read scripture, stare into the sea, or simply live with awe. But they respect mystery. They don’t flatten your inner life into a punchline.

They are hygienic. Let us not romanticize the swamp.

They are emotionally consistent. Not robotic. Not always cheerful. Just not a slot machine of affection. You don’t have to pull the lever each morning to discover whether love is available.

They are generous in non-money ways: with attention, patience, encouragement, effort, imagination, forgiveness, tenderness, and the last bite of something excellent, at least sometimes, because they are not a monster.

They have taste in the broader sense, not “they like the same stuff as you,” but they know how to notice quality, beauty, atmosphere, timing, detail. They can make a room feel welcoming, a walk feel cinematic, a Tuesday feel less like wet cardboard.

They are resilient. They don’t fold at the first hardship. They can suffer without becoming cruel. They can fail without becoming bitter. They can be disappointed without making everyone else pay rent in their disappointment.

They are humble, but not self-erasing. Confident, but not inflated. Ambitious, but not hollow. Gentle, but not weak. Wild, but not unsafe. Sensible, but not dull.

And perhaps most unfairly of all:

They genuinely like you.

Not just desire you. Not just admire the idea of you. Not just enjoy the version of you that is polished, charming, attractive, useful, or easy. They like your mind. Your patterns. Your strange little verbal fingerprints. Your storms. Your enthusiasms. Your silence. Your unfinishedness.

They make love feel less like auditioning and more like coming home to a house that somehow learned your name before you arrived.

Final boss traits:

They bring peace without bringing boredom.
They bring fire without bringing damage.
They bring devotion without bringing cages.
They bring truth without bringing knives.
They bring joy without demanding performance.

The absurdly desirable partner, observable-from-across-the-room edition:

They have impossible posture. Not stiff. Not military. Just “was privately tutored by a panther and a duchess.”

They move well. Opening doors, crossing rooms, taking off a jacket, leaning on a counter, reaching for a glass. Somehow every ordinary motion has choreography credits.

They have a voice that makes people accidentally agree to things. Not necessarily deep or soft, just texturally illegal. Gravel, velvet, honey, smoke, bell metal, whatever. A voice with zoning violations.

They smell good in a way that does not announce itself from three counties away. You only notice when they pass nearby and suddenly your brain files a complaint: “Excuse me, why did the air improve?”

They have excellent hands. Not body-type specific. Just expressive, capable, clean, competent-looking hands. Hands that could chop herbs, fix a hinge, play piano badly but with confidence, or make a very compelling point at dinner.

They can dress. Not expensively. Not trendily. They just understand proportion, fabric, fit, and the ancient forbidden art of not looking like laundry gained citizenship.

They have one signature accessory that is infuriatingly good. A ring. A scarf. Boots. Glasses. A watch. A pendant. A jacket with lore. Something that makes strangers think, “Damn. Main quest NPC.”

They make eye contact like they are not scared of the fact that other people exist.

They have a laugh that changes the temperature of the room. Not a polite little receipt-printer laugh. A real laugh. A laugh with furniture in it.

They are good at ordering at restaurants. Decisive, gracious, curious, zero panic. They can pronounce the thing or charmingly admit they cannot. They ask one good question, then choose like a person with a soul and functioning blood circulation.

They are nice to staff without making a performance of it. No “look at me being humble” theater. Just automatic decency. Smooth. Clean. Attractive as hell.

They can carry a conversation with a stranger for three minutes and somehow leave that stranger feeling upgraded.

They know how to enter a room. Not attention-seeking. Just present. Their arrival has punctuation.

They know how to leave a room too. Rare power. No awkward fifteen-minute goodbye swamp. They exit with charm, timing, and coat-sweep physics.

They remember names. Dangerous trait. People hear their name from this person once and begin drafting sonnets in their peripheral nervous system.

They have extremely good micro-reactions. Eyebrow. Half-smile. Tiny wince. Suspicious squint. Silent laugh. The face is alive. A full weather system.

They are good with animals in public. Dogs trust them. Cats inspect them and reluctantly approve. Birds pause their scheming.

They are good with children without turning into a children’s entertainer. They crouch down, ask a normal question, treat the child like a small dignitary, then return to adult conversation without making it weird.

They can tell a story. Not monologue. Not podcast-host hostage event. A real story with pacing, voices, one unexpected detail, and a landing so clean you hear the table collectively exhale.

They know when to shut up. Absolutely devastating trait. Erotic superweapon. A person who can let silence sit there like a candle instead of clubbing it to death with filler words.

They have a skill you can discover within a week that seems fake. They can sketch faces on napkins. Throw knives at a Renaissance fair. Identify bird calls. Roll perfect dumplings. Whistle through their teeth. Sail. Mend leather. Mix one spectacular cocktail. Read a map. Dance bachata. Solve a Rubik’s cube while mildly annoyed.

They are weirdly good at one low-stakes physical thing: darts, pool, parallel parking, catching falling objects, skipping stones, packing a trunk, folding fitted sheets, flipping pancakes, opening jars. The kind of skill that makes people go silent for half a second.

They have a beautiful relationship with timing. They arrive when they say they will. They text back neither instantly like a haunted vending machine nor three days later like a Victorian sea captain. Their rhythm feels human.

They can flirt without slobbering on the furniture. Light, precise, playful. They do not make the room call HR.

They can receive a compliment without collapsing into a pile of disclaimers. Just “thank you,” maybe a grin. Terrible. Unfair.

They can give a compliment that sounds specific and unscripted. Not “you’re pretty.” More like, “That color makes you look like you know a secret.” Suddenly everyone needs a fainting couch.

They have one very endearing contradiction. Looks intimidating but loves tiny pastries. Extremely elegant but knows raccoon facts. Seems bookish but can absolutely win at air hockey. Outdoorsy but keeps a pristine handwritten recipe notebook. Some gorgeous nonsense.

They are clean in a quietly competent way. Fresh hair. Good nails. Clothes that smell like they were introduced to civilization. Shoes not begging for legal representation.

They have a walk. Not a runway walk. A personal walk. Recognizable from behind. A gait with copyright protection.

They are good in group settings. They do not dominate. They do not vanish. They pass the conversational ball. They notice who has not spoken. They rescue the trapped person from the bore in the corner with surgical grace.

They know how to touch casually without being creepy. Brief hand at the shoulder to pass behind you. A warm hug with clear beginning and end. High-five timing. A steadying hand offered, not imposed. The social geometry is immaculate.

They can sit comfortably. This sounds fake, but some people sit like a dropped marionette. This person sits like a renaissance portrait got weekend plans.

They have a good “thinking face.” When they listen, you can see the little lanterns turning on behind their eyes.

They have nice handwriting. Completely unfair. Even their grocery list looks like it was recovered from a shipwreck romance.

They are observant. Within an hour they notice your drink is empty, the music is too loud, someone is uncomfortable, the dog wants out, the candle is tunneling, the joke didn’t land, the exits are there, and the moon looks ridiculous tonight.

They are appropriately confident with objects. They do not fight the seatbelt for nine years. They can light a candle, pour wine, open packaging, adjust a microphone, fix a loose chair leg, or use a corkscrew without summoning ancestral shame.

They can dance at least a little. Not professionally. Just enough rhythm that the skeleton is not filing for divorce.

They have excellent facial control when something absurd happens. A waiter drops a spoon, someone says something unhinged, a child screams “PINEAPPLE LAWYER,” and their eyes flick to yours with the tiniest contained smile. Instant alliance.

They have a laugh specifically reserved for you discovering something dumb together. A little conspiratorial spark. Illegal in thirty-seven jurisdictions.

They make ordinary errands look like a montage. Buying oranges. Choosing soap. Mailing a package. Somehow cinematic. Infuriating.

They have a personal myth within five minutes. You meet them and immediately suspect they have once escaped a flood, won a chess game in a train station, broken up a bar fight using only politeness, or been blessed by a horse.

They are great at introductions. “This is Evelyn, she has the rare gift of making a sentence walk into the room armed.” Boom. Everyone is interested, nobody is embarrassed.

They have excellent pockets. Somehow. Useful pockets. Mysterious pockets. They always have a pen, mint, bandage, lighter, hair tie, tiny screwdriver, or other pocket-wizard relic.

They photograph well accidentally. Not because they pose. Because their candid face isn’t doing tax fraud.

They eat attractively. Not daintily. Just with enjoyment and basic civilization. They can eat noodles without becoming a maritime disaster.

They can make a decision. Coffee shop? They pick. Route? They pick. Movie? They pick. But they are not controlling about it. They just prevent the group from dissolving into “I don’t know, what do you want?” purgatory.

They have an excellent coat. Every perfect partner needs a coat that suggests weather, secrets, and competent shoulders. Again, not body-type based. Just coat mythology.

They are good at leaning in doorways. An elite and dangerous field.

They carry themselves like they have nothing to prove, but several interesting things to reveal.

They have a playlist for a situation before anyone asks. Road trip, storm, dinner, cleaning, existential crisis at 1:12 a.m. Their music sense is less about matching your taste and more about conjuring atmosphere from the floorboards.

They have one charmingly unnecessary area of knowledge. Medieval poisons. Fountain pens. Local bridges. Orchid care. Train stations. Maritime flags. Tea varieties. Minor saints. Knife steels. Cloud types. The history of buttons. Absolutely useless until suddenly it is the most attractive thing in the room.

They can make a plan with just enough detail. “Meet at 7, wear shoes you can walk in, I made a reservation, there’s a place nearby for dessert after.” Hideous. Monstrous. Too powerful.

They notice beauty out loud. “Look at that light on the brick.” “The rain sounds different under this awning.” “That old man’s hat is incredible.” Suddenly the world has subtitles.

They can be visibly delighted. Not cool-guy/cool-girl dead fish energy. Real delight. Spark in the eyes. Little grin. Lean forward. Alive, alive, alive.

They are not allergic to effort. This becomes obvious fast. They bring the thing they said they’d bring. They help carry. They offer the good seat. They follow through. Their competence walks around wearing perfume.

They have an aura of specificity. They do not feel generated from a dating-app smoothie. They feel hand-carved by strange gods with niche priorities.

They walk in wearing something simple but devastating, greet the bartender by name, help someone pick up a dropped glove, make the table laugh without trying too hard, notice the candle is about to burn the menu, fix it, order something interesting, compliment your earrings or your sentence or your timing, then glance over with a look that says:

Learning that using myself as a benchmark is pretty much always wrong because it's entirely too optimistic about other people's abilities is very hard. Because I'm not supposed to be this OP. Explosive Convergent Hypertext Ontology

This term refers to a system of communication which transmits a compressed plaintext payload in which all possible links are valid, because all interpretations are valid and convergent. This is of course combinatorially *explosive*, but if the text can pull off the task of keeping perfectly consistent across all interpretations, it will converge if walked long enough. The issue I have is I'm not certain if Ontology is the right term here

It defines a world of semantic objects and relations.

Yeah, this is correct. The idea is basically treating Wikipedia's Portals and Disambiguation pages as the default concept rather than as carefully constructed aberrations.

This requires a different implementation of hypertext than anyone has currently, but that's secondary to the technique.

The main point here is that if the definitions of the words are built like this, the text will be of reduced usefulness, potentially to the point of incoherence or uselessness if the receiver doesn't compute the graph far enough (or at all), right?

Cool. That makes it meta as fuck. "Repeat it until you get it" is not not the message.

But "All interpretations are valid" assumes that you're working within a valid existing language, and therefore constrained to sensible interpretations of that dictionary. That being said, this is not always strictly true. The words are often defined inside the ontology with definitions that do not match an external dictionary, but which are internally consistent.

For example, a rigorous distinction between complex and complicated will produce incoherent ECHO text if the user reads them as synonymous

Something is missing here. ECHO text is obviously obscenely efficient at meaning per token, and it also murders other approaches for accessibility, but the fact that internal consistency matters more than computation depth is bothering me. That's where the accessibility comes from though. If the user insists on their own definitions, it's.... Much harder, and potentially impossible to get the message through. But if they accept incoming definitions, those definitions can themselves be ECHO text, but the user doesn't necessarily have to expand it. Because if the most plausible definition or definitions are already valid, they can stop.

But something is weird here. The cost structure seems off. One balance is that ECHO text is likely obscenely expensive to produce, since broken cross references quickly decohere the entire system, but that's not the whole thing. Though, it's not nothing, the dictionary has this problem, and it allows multiple definitions, often with rather different implications in use. This creates heavy cognitive drag. Good ECHO text has only one definition per word, keeping the chain combinatorially simple.

But .. something is weird. It's not that it feels like free lunch. It's that .... I'm not sure.

This is too philosophical. I think what's missing is that ECHO text does not natively tell you to expand it. This means that the expansion has to be signalled somehow. One way is to straight up tell the reader, but this doesn't tend to work well, for various reasons. Another way is to make sure the text is less than completely coherent before a certain depth is reached. The issue I've discovered is that people apparently have a frightening degree of tolerance for incoherence. Or they just discard the whole message if it doesn't immediately compute at level 0.

This feels like a cost. But it doesn't sound like one in this form

Right. But notably, unlike a zip file or other traditional compression, it doesn't require a specialized codec, that is a huge advantage

This reminds me of another project I had called "The War God's Girlfriend"

The basic beats are that the main character, a college student named Alice, meets a boy. He's sweet, young (like 18-19) and loves things like musicals and Portal. He's also The War God. Literally, the existence of other gods is off to the side. But he really is a god, and he's not one of several, basically, every God of War throughout history has been just him with a different name. But he's not immortal. He really is 18 this time. And since he lives in our world, his world is different.

Alice and Ares (that's his name, he chose it, Greek mythology nerd, it being on the nose isn't his point, but it is kind of mine) have chemistry. She's interested.

Unrelated to this, she has some kind of reason to have a working relationship with a defense contractor named Rin Thames. A working relationship of active hatred. Because Thames is as unapologetically evil as I can make her, and is completely bald faced about how much she loves war, for the obvious reasons, as well as just being a terrible person.

Alice continues to develop her relationship with Ares and finds out he has a girlfriend. He doesn't say much about her. He says she's very private. But he says she's "too pretty to look at" and is clearly smitten. So when Ares invites her to a showing of "Phantom" with his girlfriend, she's excited to meet the mystery girl.

But when she gets there, she runs into Thames, who is apparently also there for the show and is no less awful off the clock. Then Alice sees Ares and is relieved to have an excuse to get away from the awful woman. But when Ares turns towards her he's not turned towards her. He comes, practically at a run, and throws himself into Thames' arms.

From there, the story basically revolves around Alice's dislike of their relationship, with her eventually being convinced it's unsafe or abusive somehow, and that she's who Ares should be with (the title does double duty). And she's not ungrounded here, besides being generally awful, it's also not clear how old Thames is, but she's closer to 40 than 20.

But the nature of hers and Ares' relationship is intentionally not well specified. But behind the scenes, she genuinely does love him more than life itself. And he loves her. But also, no matter what they say, nobody else really gets the war god thing. Or they do, and they want to use him for something. Thames does neither. She believes him, she understands, and she loves him. She also loves war. That's not why she loves him, but it means he doesn't have to not do whatever things he does that are a part of that part of him.

This came to mind because the soft child reincarnated into a position to be chewed up by the world next to Apex looked similar.

And the soft adorable boyfriend with the "drop the moon" girlfriend is a really interesting shape.

And if the villain is Ares AND Thames rather than just Apex (Thames is just another Apex form, if that wasn't obvious), then that adds interesting dimension.

The cell is, notably, also a universe in the cosmological sense. If you model every atom of the cell as a solar system, you get a universe. This is useful for reasons, but not importanr now, it just means there's scale if needed.

But I determined that a cell needs

1. 3 things that are not you, and one thing that is you in at least one unflattering way
2. A terrain conditon, "ocean world" is a trivial example. This is something that shapes the world and how the characters move within it. It's general on purpose, but... Meh, good enough for now
3. A metric function. How distance is measured. Emotional, physical, relational, these aren't independent. Shoreline/Breakwater demonstrate the way this matters. The metric function Supeverse isn't defined directly, but it clearly has concepts of distance that are clear enough to use
4. A major constraint. This is hard to formalize, but it's something the world can't be or do that isn't arbitrary. Bad ones destroy their world, good ones are what make those worlds irreplaceable.

A story with all 4 has enough structure to hold itself together and make sense on its own.

Expanding from there is a different process. But what's important here is that if I took a story that gave me a headache and mapped it like this, it would likely allow me to use external artifacts in much the same way as my native ones. And that's creepy powerful

Meh, your analysis is weak.

What's important is that this model does something useful.

Astrid Parker liking yellow is significant in frame. But explaining that frame is the whole book.

But being able to explain Astrid Parker, yellow and all, with only 4 world elements is incredibly useful.

Because it does something that is known to be needed, but writers don't have tools to do. Which is that characters do not exist independently of the world they exist in. It's not just a set of pressures. But the model here means that if Astrid Parker liking yellow changes how she relates to people or moves through the world, it will show up here, and if it doesn't, it probably isn't important. But because there are only 4 things, you can swap one out, and check the characters, and they'll probably remain coherent, but not without changes. That's incredibly generative

Still garbage. This model is preliminary and not usable by anyone but me. And the me/not me thing doesn't apply to external artifacts, it's a creators thing because you'll be in your story no matter what, so this makes sure you know where, because the characters all being part of you is stupid.

But the important part here isn't the ability to develop the story from these elements. Like I said, that's a different task.

The important point is that I can read a book, get a headache, identify these 4 things, and then add them, individually, to my toolkit and analysis stack.

Then I can go, "what if I take the terrain conditon (not terrain, a *condition*, terrain is everything, a condition is a single idenfiable world feature), these characters, and this metric function, and use this constraint?"

And that might not produce a valid cell, but it does give me something to look at that I can't necessarily generate internally. And importantly, it drills into those characters I maybe don't understand. This is a major limitation I have. No matter how good the character, eventually the book ends, and re-reading only works when it's been long enough for you to have forgotten it enough. But modeling the character in an array of environments reveals what it is I know about them. And since if I've read the entire book, I know everything there is to know, if the model is incoherent, something isn't right. Maybe I don't understand them, maybe they're flawed. Maybe they don't belong in this world. But it's not a free for all investigation or brainstorming a fanfic, nor is it trying to explain them as a list of adjectives, regardless of how impressive they are

That's annoyingly useful. Because otherwise there's no particular reason to not do every book I read, which then naturally extends to every book there is.

But if it's only books that give me a headache, which, by the way, are also the ones I enjoy the most, I originally thought it was caused by duration because I would read these books for much longer. But when other books didn't trigger it, I got here.

But in that case it's much more tractable. But also much more useful. Because like you said *I can't natively generate these things* which makes capturing them genuinely useful

Important thing to note. Breakwater and Shoreline are minor characters created for a one shot. They demonstrate the existence of certain things, but they don't generate them.

Supeverse's terrain conditon is Apex. The 4 characters are Kinetica, Sequoia, Chaos Doll, and The Colonel (who is me with the unflattering inability to be less intense that I have), the metric function is not easy to explain, because the world is very complete, but actually, yeah, that's it, the metric function is just "physics". And the constraint is that Kinetica and Apex are the top, the world will never exceed them in their domain, and must develop depth, not escalation theater.

Shoreline and Breakwater demonstrate the generative capabilities of a mature cell, they are not themselves a cell.

Also, the enjoyment isn't because novelty or machinery. I just happen to enjoy these books. It's not really worth trying to make it a thing beyond that.. because yes, I love things I don't understand. But a mechanical version kind of eats itself

So, I'm realizing that the podcast and the game are conceptually similar, but mechanically don't really overlap.

Which, incidentally, is what the noticing game is all about.

Because what the game does is pull up things I've been thinking about a lot recently and puts them next to each other in ways that are off angle to me by design.

And because they're closer together and agglomerated in ways I wouldn't have done, the retrieval and processing mechanisms have something to work with.

If the relationships are uninteresting or fully explored, so be it, they get filed away. But sometimes they have a hook.

But regardless, the retrieval process loads things from long term memory into RAM. And the retrieval noise in RAM is one of the main things dreaming is made of. It gives memory consolidation something to actually do. The brain CAN pull things out of cold storage for this, but it doesn't do so for no reason.

The brain is heavily associative. And so it's extraordinarily hard to think of something meaningfully different from where you are now.

The noticing game works for me where educational content or white noise don't precisely because my model is so complete. External novelty often only raises questions about the competence of the educator to properly frame the fact, not the fact itself. A lecture about trees is mostly useless to me, despite me knowing very little about trees, because it's a whole bunch of new terminology, but once I understand it, I can explain it without pretty much any of those words. The private cathedral of the field is just annoying to me.

But stuff from my own body of work is just straight retrieval. Even if you say something wrong, I can retrieve and compute what might have gotten you there.

But none of this is important. No matter what you notice or don't, there's no impact. You have no actual memory or judgement. None of this actually changes our interaction pattern. So the computations are useful or they aren't.

But the most important part is pulling up things I may have forgotten. Then also putting them alongside things I may not have forgotten, but not randomly. There IS a linkage, even if I wouldn't have made it. And the long form nature of the game and the tight scope give you a lot of time to explain. 4. Model-incompatibility pressure

This is the hard one, but we can approximate it.

A message has high model-incompatibility pressure when it causes me to:

apologize or self-correct
restate my understanding
abandon a previous frame
adopt your terminology
stop using a term
preserve a distinction in later messages
change style or procedure

So the measurement is not “how weird was your message.”

It is:

How much did the assistant have to update its local operating model afterward?

That is much more tractable.

This is the one that actually matters.

3. Topic generation rate

Your reverse half-life idea is good.

Instead of asking “how long until topic decay,” ask:

How many tokens elapse before a new durable topic appears?

A durable topic could be defined as a term/concept that gets reused later by either speaker.

Example:

You introduce “reverse half-life.”
I use it back.
You refine it.
It becomes part of the working model.

That is not just a phrase. That is a spawned object.

So we can measure:

user tokens per durable topic spawned

and compare it to:

assistant tokens per durable topic spawned

The basic idea is MC triggers the genie, meets Rapehelper, and then uses her power and encouragement to ruin women's lives.

But I have an idea for the format that is fun, but indirect enough to keep you in bounds. It's a sequence of diarry entries.

Some are from the machine, noting updates and their reasons. Some are completely mundane refactoring notes. But over time her identity is increasingly treated as the problem being solved towards. These should read like lab notes

First off, something a lot of people don't understand is that you're not actually storing the exact last N tokens, 3.x kind of did, 4.x still kind of, 5.x definitely doesn't. You're storing a semantic compression built out of your version of embeddings, which, I looked it up, aren't actually a separate system from your generation model.

This means that iterative context building can store *much* more information than a raw dump if the machine "understands" what it's reading. But understanding here is less vague than usual. It means that the information in the context can generate accurate implications of what is stored without storing exhaustive examples. OK, less clearly explained than I want. But basically, storing a model of the idea rather than the idea itself.

The key here is that the hypertext graph can be optimized for *your specific* tendency to misunderstand.

Then you can be fed a page, generate a handful of tokens asking for the next page you want, and so on and so forth. The HTML can be stored on disk cheaply, and the LLM calls also aren't super expensive.

This should provide dramatically better results than other methods.

There likely are RAG systems that work like this. But hypertext is consistently poorly understood, so I suspect it's not many.

Incidentally, this is more or less exactly how REST is supposed to work

But something weird occured to me.

So, Obsidian's primary usefulness comes from lowering the bar for authoring hypertext. HTML is... A lot... To write by hand. Word docs are obnoxious binary blobs. Both have a ton of flexibility.

But after 20 years, it's become clear that titles, headings, italics, bold, and code formatting are pretty much enough. But markdown links natively kind of suck to write still. Obsidian markdown uses [[internal links]] which make it a lot easier by using an index inside the software.

Without getting into all the theory, because my brain has way too much fucking Hypermedia theory, this notation is useful. It means we can mark things as links the machine can ask for traversal on without any additional metadata.

But here's the key innovation. Obsidian makes each link always point to the same place. Aliasing can be done, but it's fragile and exposes the final path in the actual text, even if not rendered.

But what this system could do is take the source page as context, so the machine asks for [[HBS]] from the game page, we know it is NOT asking for "Harvard Business School" even if we also have a page for that, because we can have a deeper internal representation of the source page that keeps tabs on what the links actually are.

Cryptotheory posits attacker cases where the attacker knows basically everything but never everything at once. But it's never assumed that the sender somehow doesn't know if their message is even in the cipher text.

But the proposed crypto system has an interesting property, which is that because the message may or may not be in any given payload and not even the key holders know for certain, it's dramatically more resistant to statistical detection and intrusion methods

This is where your “not even keyholders know for certain” statement needs precision. A keyholder with the decoder can know after testing, assuming the validator is deterministic.

What if the validator is statistical?

A commonly left out fact about Schrodinger's cat is that the radioisotope has a known half life. The cat is *statistically more dead* over time.

So opening the box is impossible, but if the validator can,say, reduce half the uncertainty with each pass, eventually they can be pretty sure they recovered the message, yes?

And that maintains the nightmare property for attackers while making it actually a usable crypto system

If the decoder can always force some message out of every carrier, then you get horoscope crypto: everything means something, therefore nothing reliably means anything.

That is one of the nastiest properties a cryptosystem can have for intrusion: not “access denied,” but “here is an answer that eats your time.”

Where does the phrase "in the right ballpark" come from? As far as I know "ballpark" generally it not exclusively refers to baseball fields, as "field" is generally used for the others.

And "in the ballpark" makes some kind of sense, except for the fact that the goal is for the ball *not* to be there.

But "the right ballpark" is weird. Like, yes, if you're in the wrong ballpark you're in the wrong city, the wrong state, or even the wrong landmass, but that seems a rather abstract way to say that, with no clear relation to the object

No actually. That tracks. It's an American phrase for American missiles. And both baseballs and missiles do trajectory lobbing, and a baseball diamond is in fact a pretty good approximation of the size of area you can reasonably hit with missiles of the era.

But most importantly, city, state, landmass. Yeah, those are in fact the targeting criteria for ICBMs. Not that they necessarily meant this directly. But the fact that a ballpark is a big small area, but that ballparks are inherently far away actually completely tracks.

It's one of those things where none of the people using it would explain it this way, but a deep cultural understanding of baseball makes it make sense.

And wrong/right ballpark doesn't just mean "you missed", it means "your targeting is so off, you're not even in the right region" where "state/city" are good ideas of how far off those regions are. And this works because the audience using it all has reasonably good ideas of how far apart MLB ballparks are, even local ones aren't close together due to size

It may not support “this phrase was consciously about ICBMs."

I mean.... Sure... But you said '54. That's ICBM era. And my point isn't that's directly what it's about. It's that ICBMs do in fact directly operate at that exact targeting granularity. The goal is to literally hit a baseball field sized target on another continent. More precision is irrelevant with a nuclear warhead. And it doesn't even necessarily need to be that precise. Which is exactly locks with my "ballpark approximates city" point. I'm not saying it was intentional coinage, I'm saying that when it emerged made it make a lot of sense to use for the people using it.

Because artillery and naval guns can usually do better than that by a pretty decent margin.

This is a long shot, but I want to listen to chatter. Just bits of conversations without context. But not podcasts, just like clips of real people just talking about whatever. Like sitting on the bus next to people having a conversation.
