No I'm not looking for texture. That's easy, I'm looking for the wandering of minds not my own mediated through interaction. People conversing casually are doing something with information that's rather weird.

I just spent like an hour on the bus listening to a pair of college girls wander from talking about boys ("he doesn't make an effort, he's all nonchalant, I want chalant" I looked it up, the origin is French, as far as I can tell, chalant means "guarded", which seems incoherent, but it isn't completely, and gives an interesting angle on things to make it coherent), to recycling, (also about boys, but the phrase was "reduce (ego), reuse (between girls), recycle" but what struck me is that most things degrade through this process, and must eventually find a permanent home or be destroyed, this is not incorrect of duck boys), to astrology (pulled on thoughts about timing, astronavigation, triangulation, and Kepler for me), to food ("Rice porridge is good, but only if it's savory"), to clothes ("if you gave me a choice between unlimited money and all the clothes in the world, I'd pick the clothes, but only in my size").

It's not that I can't have these thoughts, it's not even the order. It's actually the *lack* of depth that is most valuable here. That's not my normal (or ever) operating mode, but the medium of casual conversation acts as a .... I'm not quite sure how to describe it, not enough data. But the fact of two participants whose primary goal is neither communication, agreement, or knowledge, but rather the act of interaction itself creates channel properties not observable in formal systems.

But despite riding the bus regularly, this doesn't actually happen all that often naturally. I'm trying to find a source that is less chance dependent

Right, Webster is the dictionary I consulted as well.

"French, from Old French, from present participle of nonchaloir to disregard, from non- + chaloir to concern, from Latin calēre to be warm — more at lee"

Lee:
"Definition (Entry 1 of 2)
1: protecting shelter
2: the side (as of a ship) or area that is sheltered from the wind
adjective
Definition (Entry 2 of 2)
1: of, relating to, or being the side sheltered from the wind
— compare weather
2: facing in the direction of motion of an overriding glacier —used especially of a hillside"

It's not precisely clear how these words are related, but they are, and "nonchalant" in usage, does actually mean something closer to "unguarded" than "uncaring".

The thing about "I want chalant", in this reading is that she's not saying she wants him guarded/sheltered *from* her. She's saying she wants him guarded/sheltered *with regards to her*. It's messy, but she's mangling a word on purpose, that's expected. But this is how language actually emerges and evolves. This is the kind of thing you can't properly do synthetically, at least not without studying enough examples to separate real cases from arbitrary random recombination.

And yeah, it is random walk like, but it's not random at all, that's the key

Here's a description of Convexplore:

convexplore

convexplore is a small personal reading tool for re-entering large conversation archives without treating them like books, search results, or chat logs.

The basic unit is the sentence. Instead of opening a massive transcript and scrolling through hundreds of pages, the user is shown a small set of sentence fragments from their own messages. Each fragment is just enough to catch interest without demanding commitment. This creates a low-pressure “find a door” flow: glance, notice something live, tap into it.

The app has two modes.

In explore mode, convexplore shows three short one-line excerpts. These are not summaries or titles. They are baited handles: small pieces of the original text, pulled from the middle of a sentence, meant to preserve the flavor of the thought while staying easy to scan. A reroll control replaces them with another set when none of the current options catches.

Tapping an excerpt enters traversal mode at that exact sentence. Traversal mode shows one sentence at a time, preserving the original conversational sequence. Speaker identity is carried by color rather than labels, keeping the screen clean and letting the text remain central. Normal left/right taps move backward or forward one sentence. Additional controls allow jumping to the previous or next speaker, which helps move across long turns without losing the surrounding conversation structure.

The important UX idea is that convexplore separates discovery from reading. Explore mode is for finding a thread worth entering. Traversal mode is for walking that thread sentence by sentence once interest has been established.

It is not designed to replace full transcript reading, search, or summarization. It is designed for reactivation: finding a thought that still has charge, then giving the user enough local context to decide whether to keep following it. The app treats the archive as a navigable field of remembered thinking rather than a document to consume from beginning to end.

I have recently become very aware of the nearly exclusive representation of lesbians in my fiction and I don't know what to do about that. Because it's unrealistic. And when there are only lesbians you lose contrast.

But I don't like men. Not as in I dislike men. As in, I've dated men. I've dated enough men. Good. Done.

Male characters are not desire objects to me. Nor are they something I can see through.

I understand men a great deal more than most women. But I am not a man. That becomes clearer every year. There are things about men I fundamentally don't get. Though that is in part due to my general lack of understanding of humans.

But what's annoying is that it's not a total blindness. It's that I can't instantiate the *bad* parts of humans. I can make shitty girls, kind of, though I have blind spots. But shitty guys... Not so much. I especially can't generate any of the shitty behaviors they exhibit towards women, such as non commitment, flakiness, "bros before hoes", and other gender difference weirdness.

I get how men are different. But I can't *inhabit* that version of reality without distorting it. This is exactly what makes me so attractive to the right people, but it's inconvenient in fiction form

Two things. First. They do need to be desire objects sometimes. At least some of my girls need to be actually bi onscreen, or, God forbid, actually, genuinely only attracted to men.

Second, you're suggesting that I paint the surface and not run the underlying machinery.

Not only is that not how I work. It's weak and burns out fast while producing weak, stale, shallow characters.

The actual reality is that even people with low interiority make sense inside their own motivational structure. And when you can understand, generate, and inhabit that structure mechanically, the character does 3 things

1. They open a window into people who do this, because you're not judging from the outside, you are doing exactly as they are, justifying from inside the machinery
2. They gain the ability to surprise you when forces conspire to put their worldview to the test in a way they aren't prepared for
3. They feel realistic and justified, even and especially when they do exceptionally shitty things. These stop being writing fiat to milk emotional stakes, they are actually born from that characters motivational structure, and so they're much more real

You get none of that when you make cardboard cutouts

I realized something as I was thinking about this.

My characters may be attractive. But they specifically *aren't* there for audience approval. In fact, I constantly demand that they be *less* likeable and *more* horrifying or unsettling.

Essentially, I write myself as the villain. And I think that's why it keeps working so well. Because fiction really doesn't have many good villains.

Black Panther is supposedly good, I disagree, but whatever. Killmonger is supposedly a good villain, I disagree, but whatever. But the second point is the main given reason for the first point.

The movie sparked a big discussion about the role of the villain in giving the story shape and meaning. And how lacking it so often is.

The issue with most villains is that their authors don't understand them, usually because they're too pansy to commit to the kinds of things the villain canonically does. So the villain ends up as a cardboard cutout, or has some obnoxiously legible motivation like being an ecoterrorist (this is the plot of the new Godzilla AND the Avengers, just to name two), or their mom/dad never loved them enough.

The villain is never actually doing the evil thing on purpose. They're always doing it as a means to an end. It's dumb. Even the old reliable of villain generators, Nazis, has gone stale because society is too pansy to handle a character who actually believes those things. Though, tbh, I don't completely disagree. But The Red Skull is a great villain precisely because he takes the core Nazi thing, but he's not technically a Nazi, so he can be his own thing.

But Skynet is a great example. The villain is either a faceless thing that is doing the plot because that's it's nature and it essentially doesn't know better. Or it's a poor baby human who really just needs a hug. Or it's the first one dressed up as the second one and it has both sets of problems.

Meanwhile, every Apex character is specifically designed so that no matter how deep you look for tje nuggety center, you'll only find them more disturbing. And it's precisely the fact that they aren't all bad that makes this work. It's the fact that they're consistently capable of meaningful affection in certain directions, and that's enough for them. It's the fact that they consistently classify their victims as irrelevant. Not as collateral damage, just... Dirt. And they mean it.

A lot of villains try for this, but their one sided motivation makes it ring hollow.

Right. But I mean villain/antagonist literally in the narrative sense.

My characters aren't the protagonist. Notice that? They're consistently narrated through limited observation.

Good Conduct is a bit of an exception, but in the hero/villain model Audrey is the Thing to be Saved, her friends are the hero team, and Optima is the villain.

But this is where the "subject the world to me" becomes clearest.

Because Apex characters have frighteningly well developed worldviews and consistently exist specifically to pressure test the hero's concept of moral correctness.

The stories that emerge are consistently driven by the fact that the Apex villain closes off the exits to a clean moral victory. She consistently produces a world where winning, if it's even possible, requires doing horrifying things that may be justifiable, but which even the act of justification proves are not all that clean.

And what further makes it work is that Apex villains aren't invulnerable in a flat fiat way, but because they're not designed to lose, they aren't easy to beat.

And that makes the heroes actually have a serious issue, and actual uphill fight, real loss as the most likely outcome. Which in turn translates into real stakes

Notably, The Joker in The Dark Knight works exactly like this. Various times, but the Ferry Sequence is the best example.

Batman is doing Batman things the whole time. But an entire ferry full of people could blow up at any time without him OR Joker deciding anything. It's up to a bunch of normal people who can't communicate. Thus producing a deliciously literal Prisoner's Dilemma

The scene forces morality under pressure and asks "No 3rd option, what do you do?"

But this ties to my larger point of why it consistently produces stronger fiction than it's starting point.

Because villains/antagonists, by design and definition, *act*. They change things, challenge norms, shake things up. Often violently. A hero also changes things, but he's accountable for the harm done along the way, and so his blast radius is constrained. A villain, on the other hand, gets better (to a point) the more violently indifferent to the harm they are.

And again, because my villains aren't cartoons I invent to lose, they are in fact just a carve out of me (who, to your point, do take on a life of their own, which is important), they always *have a point*. And it's usually about agency, which is exactly what enables the villain things, but it's also "Freedom", which is supposed to be firmly in hero land.

Right. The other thing Apex villains have that a lot of villains are *supposed* to have, but rarely do is *maturity*.

Heroes are often young, even if not physically, they have that hopeful discovery driven outlook. Batman doesn't, but honestly the longer I look at him the more I realize he's weak as shit as a character, which is why he has the bat family, Alfred, AND the largest rogues gallery of anyone except maybe Spiderman, because he can't actually carry any of the story by himself.

But Apex villains, being built from me, also inherit my obnoxiously well developed world view. So they're not just doing the same things as the hero harder. They're doing it at least in part because they understand the hero better than they understand themselves.

This reminds me of something that's bothered me for years.

In whatever Star Wars movie it happens in, Yoda sends Luke into a tree, he meets Vader, kills Vader, and then the mask breaks and he sees his own face.

This is supposed to be him facing his fear.

But like... So what? Also, why does it have his face? It doesn't make any sense except as a vague "dark side tempting" thing.

But what would actually bite is if he goes into the tree and meets himself, but not recognizably himself. Maybe he's wearing the black outfit from the 3rd movie. Maybe he's wearing a mask or some shit, doesn't matter.

He attacks Luke. Luke defends himself, and it's to the death.

Then, when he prevails, he sees Vader in the mirror. The point being that this is what it feels like from the inside. That you'll continue your path and fight off attackers, but those attackers won't always be morally clean empire goons. The lesson is that righteousness isn't just what feels right. Truth isn't just what feels true. And that perhaps the most moral act is to eventually let yourself be killed (which is in fact what the real Vader does)

I'm not going to rehash it, because I have talked *a lot* about this elsewhere. But the prequels only end like they do because they're enslaved to the OT and also Lucas has a morality boner.

But basically

1. Padme is depicted as a paragon of virtue because that's how Anakin sees her. But her actual actions and context demonstrate an individual of much greater moral flexibility. Notably, Anakin says "we should do fascism", and she marries him later that week
2. Anakin, supposedly sees Kenobi step out of the ship to kill him, and instead of addressing the active threat, decides to choke out his pregnant wife who is literally the only thing in the universe he values
3. Kenobi just stands there. Not because bad writing, but because this is canonically consistent with his combat style. Waiting to let the enemy destabilize themselves. But please remember he's the one here on a murder quest, and he's the one letting an innocent die for his mission.

The braid of these show that Padme getting choked out can't make any sense, and also, that her "you're going down a path I can't follow" thing also doesn't make any sense.

The emperor has already dissolved the Senate. Democracy failed. She has already demonstrated a penchant for "aggressive negotiations". Long story short, I really don't see a version where she's *not* like "yeah let's kill the emperor and fix the galaxy correctly"

Related, the story wants you to believe the Jedi are cleanly morally pure. But they aren't. They're actually constantly at odds with The Senate. And "The Dark Side" isn't really a real thing to Padme, that's a religious thing, essentially.

And so essentially, Padme *cannot* be a huge fan of her husband's religion-job that clearly isn't good for him. And thus she's not going to frame his actions how they would. And the film actually supports this. All the shit goes down and she goes to Anakin alone, without telling anyone. She's concerned about *him*, not all the stuff she's heard. She's not neutral about all the stuff, it's a lot. But it's not her primary concern.

That is, a sufficient no-loss condition for sampling signals that do not have baseband components exists that involves the width of the non-zero frequency interval as opposed to its highest frequency component. See sampling for more details and examples.

It's annoyingly cute, but the answer really is *Sovereignty*. Slightly less cute are *Agency* and *Locality*, but those are kind of fundamentally contained within the top one, and that's the point. The core of Acknowledged is that choices matter way harder than they have any business mattering. Not because we wrote some grand epic of dialogue trees, but because where you choose to be is itself a choice, and the world mechanics constantly make that real.

Reach is part of this, it allows you to feel less helpless. Continuity is what makes it keep mattering. Adventure is the play surface, it's where the choices are made and how they feel fun. But fundamentally Acknowledged is about the fact that you can't be everywhere, and that's going to hurt sometimes, but it's also what makes anything ever matter.

For example, Dwarf Fortress can have festivals. But *you* can't be *at* the festival for exactly the same reason you can scroll through mountains. That's locality and agency right there. Sovereignty is the higher version wherein you're responsible beyond yourself. Sovereigns aren't gods like the baffling premise of Civilization famously implies. They're local, and that's what you will always feel here, for better or for worse

This gives you a course grained approximation without having to individually compute every memory individually.

Also, it's not about being "psychologically expensive", it's about the fact that the brain has pretty aggressive RAM limits and computation timeouts. Even with focus and effort you can only do so much to get around this. The brain more or less refuses to do exhaustive search.

But memory storage and retrieval, due to associative architecture, pretty much constantly does involuntary neighborhood search. This is why shower thoughts and apple on head moments happen. They "jog" your memory by creating a neighborhood that overlaps with those two bidirectional searches that terminated unfinished.

This is a very different algorithm. But it's not unmodelable

It goes:
Activate a region/neighborhood.
Let nearby associations light up.
Follow the strongest/cheapest/most available paths.
Stop when enough answer appears, the search times out, or the activation collapses.
So retrieval is not a shortest-path problem over indexed memories.

The project I'm most proud of is that we had a piece of XML that absolutely had to be correct. If it wasn't, it could tank every single stream we touched (we were the prime video live streaming team, or, one of them). We had configurations in JSON that went into a Jinja template, and we got out XML.

But this Jinja was so awful that by the time I took up the project, it was team policy that if this template was even mentioned in a ticket, that ticket could not be less than 13 points (over a week of work for a single engineer), and in practical terms, only 3 members of our 9 person team could confidently edit it. And "confidently" is a lie. The major problem was that there was no real way to know if you'd broken something unless we found out about it live in production. Because maybe you didn't break the feature you touched, maybe you broke a feature on another stream you didn't know about.

So I took the problem, normalized the inputs that were being transformed in 3 different places in 3 different scripts. Then built essentially a JSX implementation in Jinja which allowed "components" to be built and composed. Each individual component guaranteed that it was valid XML or it would error, failing rendering. And it rendered when cast to string, which allowed the objects to be placed directly in Jinja without additional handling. Also, using a little bit of introspection, if a rendering error occured, the component would self identify in the traceback. This is important because by default Jinja just says "rendering error, tough" which is super annoying when you have a 400 line template. Mine didn't give a line number, but because the components were composable, it ended up being only about a dozen possible lines that it could be once you knew the component name (which was the class name).

The two biggest wins though were in safety and verification.

First, the only thing we REALLY knew for sure was that the current version produced the correct output. And the only real way to validate a replacement was diffing against that. We used xmldiff so it wouldn't fuck up on line number differences. But if it wasn't identical, we couldn't completely verify it was right.

This is important because in theory I could have built this using an XML library or something and built the trees some other way. But ordering the elements correctly was a problem with no good solution. And XML isn't order invariant. And we couldn't be certain the receiving system was.

So during development I made sure it was exactly reproducing the same output as the legacy system.

But once my system took over. This was no longer enough.

So the system, in this case, would fetch the code from the HEAD of the main branch and run that against the code you had locally, then produce a diff.

And here's where it gets important. If you made a change, it would *always* produce a diff. And there was NO way to know if it was the right one. So I designed a review process that trained everyone on how to spot problematic looking diffs.

But most importantly, because my system was fast and reliable, the test script had a set of constants at the top of the file where you assigned stream name strings to feature name variables, and then there was a list of features (I might have used a dictionary, not important)

But when you ran the test script, it tested *every feature* every time. And so if you expected to only change feature A and feature D flagged a diff, you'd know there was an issue.

And because adding feature coverage was now as easy as changing or adding a string, adding new features or changing the benchmark stream for a feature (streams got deprecated/outdated constantly, this is live streaming) was trivial.

Once the system was live and integrated into the process, the standard allotment was 2 points (1 engineer day) and anyone on the team could do it.

The last project I worked on is really annoying to explain.

We had a lot of events from our streams. As in, literal log lines. They could be many things. But we mainly cared about "Stream Down" and "Stream Up". The streams were grouped in groups of 4, or sometimes 2, and there were regions and things that made for additional groupings.

But the main design requirement was that if all 4 origins were down simultaneously, an "outage" began. When the first one came back, it ended.

The task was to count/track these outages. But I didn't get this project as a greenfield. I inherited it as supposedly fully working. And I just had to change the data source. This was a lie. I ended up having to rebuild the entire thing by the end of it.

But there are 2 things I'm proud of.

First, the script I was given was probably the worst code I have literally ever seen in my life. And it took 4 hours to run because it was basically a nested loop comparing every line to every line.

My algorithm worked by storing "up" and "down" as booleans in a list per stream, so it was a list of 2 or 4 booleans. Then in order to compute "is_in_outage()", we summed the booleans and compared against the number of origins (which we had stored as a known value in a database that was being consumed). If the values matched, no outage, if they didn't, outage. (I don't remember which way the bits went, but it doesn't matter).

This, plus a couple other optimizations allowed me to do it in a single pass. And I could process 4x as much data in just under 10 minutes.

The other thing I did was create an "outage ID" which became the primary key for the database (the original project didn't use a database, it was a fucking disaster). The outage ID was the MD5 hash of the entire outage object (start, end, and some other data) minus the ID itself.

This ensured that the system was idempotent. You could run and upsert as many times as you wanted without duplicating entries. And since there ended up being thousands of outages, many of which were sub-second, those duplicates would quickly poison the data into soup.

OK. So we were talking about route finding algorithms, and I realized something that's been bothering me. We talked recently about Fun, Romance, and Adventure. 3 things which degrade when maximized.

But this produces a problem that looks rather route finding shaped. Assume for the moment that the system can be modeled as discrete steps and transitions. A Djikstra, A* or other pathfinding algorithm will find the shortest or lowest cost path. By the prior definition, if fun, romance, or adventure are the goal, this is the *worst* possible path.

But the best path is not the longest path, as that's possibly intractable to find and probably to walk.

That means there are likely an ensemble of very "thing" (fun, romantic, adventurous) paths, and also a lot of pretty bland ones.

This problem shape looks routing like, but it breaks a lot of the core assumptions of that space

A traditional codebook says:

4456 = red/orange
8834 = painting
9126 = cyberpunk

You need something closer to generative addressing:

a code is not looked up from a complete dictionary
a code is derived from an observation phrase, image, or annotation
the same observation process can mint or recover codes later

So maybe:

"red/orange palette" → 4456
"digital painting" → 8834
"cyberpunk hex frame" → 9126
"Japanese shrine-like architecture" → 7298
"still reflective water" → 4795

Well. Actually. You're missing an interesting thing about the happy path.

Morgan might be able to stay "a you" indefinitely. But her actual safest move is to make her exception from crating *categorical* rather than singular.

So, for example, she might get Katie/Apex to agree that "Good people don't go in crates".

Sounds easy?

Well. No.

First, they don't believe those exist.

Morgan must point out she exists.

They admit they exist, but there is only one.

Then she must *very carefully* select people she cares enough about for Katie/Apex to accept their goodness because it's important to her, but that they haven't met, and won't for some time.

Then she can start defining "good person" as a category with Katie/Apex and slowly let it engulf more people, at least theoretically.

But here's the hardest part. Morgan can push on their pushback. But she can't try to argue that any of his *current* or past toys are good people, or else the conflict becomes a problem, and he'll solve the definition in a way she won't be able to get back into.

Essentially, she needs to boil the frog backwards.

But if course, once she gets him to agree not crate good people, then she adds another category, and repeat. It never really gets easier. But the world becomes safer for her and everyone else each time.

But she can't rush. And she can't be morally repulsed by his choices. Or he won't trust her judgement. Razors edge again

No. It's not that the system protects itself. It's that "good person" isn't a native category, and none of the typical levers work by default on him. So she has to defend the theoretical goodness of a person Apex knows a lot more about, with Apex digging at maximum intensity.

That's the real issue. That this case has Apex finding that Morgan has an insufficiently rigorous definition of "good person", thus confirming his suspicion that the concept is bogus.
But if she keeps it light and abstract, he only has to engage with what she says when she says it, and she can manage the conversation depth with normal conversational tools, and this survive the encounter.

See. This is once again demonstrating why Apex is such a fantastic fucking story force.

Apex essentially works on The Superman principle.

He's *the best there is*. Maybe not always, and not in every category. But if he's good at something, he's functionally unbeatable in any practical sense. And if you aren't among the best to ever do it, you're going to get destroyed.

But he has depth, and opinions, and things he cares about, and he's convincible.

So there *is* a path. It's just that every direct one gets you killed. Force, escalation, opposition, all the usual hero tools, completely broken here. But those are actually very difficult to make good writing out of, because the muscles are imaginary and the punches don't actually happen. But routing around is intrigue, and everyone loves em some good intrigue
